subsubtopic: PORTIONS OF CBC PROGRAMS DEEMED TO BE "SUB JUDICE"
speechtext:
1.	What specific portions of the documentary film "Chasebe" were determined to be sub judice by lawyers whose advice to CBC caused the postponement of the appearance of that film on "Format 30"?
2.	Has CBC issued guidelines to its news and/or public affairs agencies indicating what matters might be considered sub judice in (a) the James Bay matter (b) any other matter?
3.	On how many previous occasions has a program been (a) changed (b) postponed (c) withdrawn because all or part of the program was deemed to be sub judice and what was (i) the name of each such program (ii) date of modification, postponement or withdrawal of each such program?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: PORTIONS OF CBC PROGRAMS DEEMED TO BE "SUB JUDICE"
speechtext:
I am
informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows: 1. The proposed presentation of the documentary film "Chissibi" on the CBC French Television Network program "Format 60" was to involve a panel discussion of the subject raised in the film; CBC's Legal Advisers found that both the voice-over commentary on the film and the subjects proposed for the panel discussion could not be legally presented at this time in view of the continuing trial.
2. CBC Program Policies which are provided to program production personnel include general guidelines on the subject to contempt of court and make the following reference to matters before the courts: "Improperly Attempting to Influence the Administration of Justice. Any comment, argument or suggestion calculated to influence the result of a trial before it is over and the appeal time has expired is contempt. For example, if a commentator comments on the evidence adduced by postulating theories as to how the crime was committed, such comment would be in contempt. It should be noted that appeals from criminal matters may be taken up to 30 days after conviction or sentence and in civil matters, up to 15 days after judgment. Even true matters may sometimes not be reported. Examples would be reports indicating that a confession has been made, or that the accused has a record. As a general rule, nothing should be reported
July 9, 1973

except that which has been admitted as evidence to the jury, or comments of judge or counsel made in front of the jury." No specific guidelines have been issued with respect to the James Bay matter; however, the CBC Legal Department has been frequently consulted concerning limitations upon programming posed by the fact of the continuing trial in this matter.
3.	The Corporation has no record of the occasions when programs have been changed, postponed or withdrawn by reason of the subject matter being sub judice. However in the news and public affairs areas, this is a matter which requires constant attention and producers throughout the Corporation consult with the Corporation's legal advisers on a daily basis to ensure that their programs do not interfere improperly with the conduct of trials by the courts.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: CLOUD SEEDING EXPERIMENTS
speechtext:
1. In western Quebec during the period 1959-63 the Meteorological Service conducted an experiment to determine whether cloud seeding with silver iodide had an effect on rainfall over that area. In the vicinity of Toronto, during the past six years, local experiments have been carried out on fog dispersal at below freezing temperatures using dry ice and liquid propane as seeding agents.
2.	The experiments were carried out as part of the Service's research program on its own account but were initiated, at least in part, by requests from other groups.
3.	No contracts or subsidies have been awarded by the Atmospheric Environment Service specifically for weather modification research. However, the Atmospheric Environment Service has participated since 1956, jointly with the Research Council of Alberta and the National Research Council, in a hail research program in Alberta aimed at increasing knowledge of the mechanisms of hail formation and eventual hail suppression or reduction of hail damage to crops. As part of this work, an annual contract for hail research was awarded to McGill University. The amount of the contract with McGill University for 1972-73 was $96,200.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
the act by which we are now governed. It was incorporated in the present legislation to take into consideration rural and urban centres of population.
Throughout the debate that took place during consideration of the act it was concluded generally that rural areas would have less population than urban areas. I know that some hon. members and, indeed, political scientists may scoff at this suggestion; they may consider it to be unjust, unfair and unreasonable: on the other hand, a number of people would argue that members of parliament represent not only the people within their constituencies but the constituencies themselves.
Here, again, I refer to the province of Alberta. Whatever formula we come up with, I think it is important that those charged with the responsibility of administering the formula do so with the spirit and intent of the act in mind. In my opinion, this has not been done in the province of Alberta where we have, under the municipal process, a majority of rural ridings containing more people than urban ridings. For example, in the province of Alberta, out of the nine rural ridings we know that as a result of redistribution five have populations well in excess of the quotient of 85,678. On the other hand, in the case of urban ridings the majority have considerably less than 85,678. We have only three constituencies which exceed that quotient, and then only by a very small margin.
It is important that whatever mechanism we devise, assurance be given that the administration is carried out with the spirit and intent of the act. I believe what has taken place in the province of Alberta is contrary to the principle and intent of the act. I should like to place on record some quotations from the debate that took place in 1963. For example, when Mr. Pickersgill introduced the legislation he pointed out as reported in Hansard of November 26, 1963, at page 5110:
It must also be pointed out to the commission that rural ridings must necessarily, in the experience of the past, have less population in general than urban ridings, and that there are other considerations, such as geographical lines, rivers, county lines and the like which must be taken into account.
Mr. Pickersgill went on to say as reported at page 5114:
We are also aware of the fact that ever since confederation, in nearly every part of Canada, the rural population has been represented by more members than the urban population. I echo the words of the right hon. gentleman a year ago when he said he did not think that could be entirely departed from.
I could quote other members who spoke during the debate, including the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), all of whom reiterated the importance of recognizing that particular aspect. There was considerable debate in respect of the tolerance figure. Figures ranging from 20 per cent to 40 per cent were suggested, and it was considered that 25 per cent would be effective. I think this underlines the importance of providing sufficient flexibility to take into account the various matters which affect persons in rural and urban centres.
We have before us in this bill a proposal by the government to solve these problems on an interim basis. I look forward to the bill achieving two things. Firstly, I believe it will provide some order and stability during these special and unique sets of circumstances. Secondly, I think

the bill recognizes a serious attempt to come up with a fairer and more just redistribution mechanism so that all areas of Canada can achieve a reasonable and equitable level of federal representation.
As a member of parliament representing a rural riding in Alberta, an agricultural area, I think I would be derelict in my duty if I failed to point out to the House that rural areas of Canada are just as important as urban centres. I certainly disapprove of the rural emasculation which has taken place in the application of the mechanism we now have. While all urban centres are overpopulated-I recognize this fact-I urge all hon. members to approach this matter on a wholly objective basis so that all Canadians can achieve the standard of representation they so richly deserve. To that end I hope this bill will be successful.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words in this debate. I believe other members from the province of Saskatchewan will be speaking but I do not think anyone has until this point. I have a number of reservations about the legislation before us, bu in spite of that I support the bill that would suspend the effect of the new electoral boundaries for 18 months while this House searches for a new formula in respect of redistribution.
Instead of talking about some of the problems or merits of this legislation I wish to suggest a special formula to replace our present senatorial floor for determining the number of seats. Before doing so, I want to say that in my province of Saskatchewan-and I think its people would agree-the commission did a fairly commendable job in redrawing the boundaries.
I wish the bill before us had been introduced two, three or fours years ago. I wish there had been changes in the formula at that time rather than now. The new boundaries could have come into effect at that time. We have in this country a census every ten years and after each census, according to our legislation, we should have a redistribution of seats. I think it is rather unjust to be debating the bill at this time. It should have been done two or three years ago in terms of population and in fairness to urban and suburban regions.
The fact is that if we do not do something about the formula at this time, provinces such as Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and in particular the northern parts of the country, will have to wait another ten years before there is an opportunity to change the boundaries on which we base representation in this House. Under the present formula many provinces will be treated very unfairly, particularly the province of Newfoundland, which will have six constituencies, with a population of 522,000. Meanwhile, New Brunswick, with a population of
120,000	more, will have ten constituencies-four members more in this House than the province of Newfoundland. The same is true of Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
I suggest the present formula for determining seats in this country is unfair. It is based on the senatorial floor of each province. New Brunswick has a senatorial floor of ten members, Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba each have six members. I think we should abolish the
July 9, 1973

senatorial floor as a method of determining the number of constituencies in the provinces with smaller populations. I believe we should have a new formula that would take into account representation by population but would also be weighted to a certain extent to the smaller provinces. I think that would better suit our democratic system. I know that many groups and associations follow the delegate theory of democracy which is weighted a bit toward the smaller groups. They send, for example, to a convention perhaps five or ten delegates for the first 100 members and from that point they use a different or diminishing formula.
I suggest, for example, that we could take a formula such as the following, which is by no means one I have tried to work out with any degree of accuracy although it is one I suggest for study. We could give to each province and to each territory-the Yukon and the Northwest Territories-automatically one member to start with, which means that the Yukon would have one seat, the Northwest Territories would have one seat and each province would have one seat as a starter. I suggest we could say that for the next 500,000 people each province would have seven members which would mean that if the population were
500,000	or less there would be a guarantee under the constitution of eight members of parliament. That would be about one member for every 62,500 people in this country. Once the figure is over half a million, the scale could become a little larger and for the next 200,000 there could be a guarantee, constitutionally, of three members. That would mean one member for every 66,700 people. Then for the next 300,000, building up to one million of population, I suggest there be guaranteed constitutionally three members. That would mean one member for every 100,000 people living within the province.
The effect of this would be to guarantee a province having a population of one million, 14 members in the House of Commons. This type of formula would be fairly rigid, but also flexible if the population of various areas increased or decreased. To give an example of how this would work out according to the present population based on the 1971 census, I find through my arithmetic that the Northwest Territories would remain with one seat as today-and the province of Prince Edward Island-here some people may argue with me-would fall, under the formula, to two seats from four; but, after all, its population is only some 112,000 according to the census of 1971.
The province of Newfoundland, under a formula of this type, would have the number of ridings go up to eight. The proposal under this legislation is six for Newfoundland, and at the present time it has seven. One can see that a formula of this type would be much more favourable to Newfoundland than to Prince Edward Island. New Brunswick, under this type of formula, would have ten constituencies, as it has today, but there would be a danger of its falling to nine. In fact, the census shows that if it should drop by 1,000 or 2,000 people, the representation of the province would go down by one seat according to the formula I have worked out. The province of Nova Scotia, under this formula, would have 11 members compared to the ten proposed in this legislation. The province of Saskatchewan from which I come, and our neighbouring province of Manitoba, would remain at 13 seats, as is the
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension case today, instead of the 12 proposed by the legislation that would become law if this bill is not passed.
If you add up the number of seats for the six smaller provinces of this country, plus the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, you find that under a formula of this sort there would be a guarantee of 59 constituencies for those less populated areas of the country. Under the legislation which will take effect if this bill does not pass, those areas would have 56 seats, or in other words three less constituencies.
I suggest that when you deal with the four larger provinces you could use the same formula or the same number as at the present time-Alberta 19, British Columbia 26, Quebec 72 and Ontario 91. If you add these together you get a total of 267 seats in this House of Commons, only three more than at present. To me it does not really matter; you could add five or ten seats in fairness to the larger provinces or in the rural areas and I do not think it would matter in the end result. I think this is the sort of formula we should have, rather than the senatorial floor which discriminates against the smaller provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland when compared with Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. In a formula like that we could have a few exceptions such as for the Northwest Territories which has a tremendously large geographical area. I think we could have two seats there. We would be justified in having two seats, despite the fact that there is a small population, because it is geographically the largest constituency in Canada, in fact so large that no member can be in all communities as often as his constituents might expect him to be.
Second, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should have a permanent speakership in the House. Mr. Speaker should represent a special constituency of the House or of Parliament Hill: I think that should be part of our electoral system. This is just one of a number of formulas that perhaps exist according to which we could apportion more fairly members of the House from various parts of the country in order to reflect the various provinces with smaller populations. It would be in accordance with the philosophy of representation by population and would also be fair to the six smaller provinces by giving them an important voice in the House.
The second concern voiced by members representing rural ridings such as mine is that the ridings are becoming very large. Under the present legislation, in many cases we have the tools that are needed in order to remedy a situation of that sort. We have a leeway of 25 per cent below and 25 per cent above the average population in a constituency. I suggest that the commission in each of the provinces, if it were to follow the rules of the game, could quite easily get around the arguments of many of us that our rural ridings are too large geographically and that because urban centres are in smaller geographical areas actually they should have more people in them than at present.
However, I do not think we need a new bill in order to meet that type of objection from members. What we could do, instead, would be to write into the bill the provision

July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension that in rural areas the commissions should be guided by the 25 per cent rule. In effect, you would have an average constituency of 60,000 to 75,000 people and an average rural seat of 90,000 to 100,000 people, with all kinds of variations in between depending on whether a riding is classified as rural or urban. Another provision that could be written into the present act 'is that in areas such as northern Ontario, Quebec and perhaps a few other northern areas of the country, the commission should take into account the rule of 25 per cent below the mean and create smaller ridings than are created under the present legislation.
Those are just a few thoughts on the redistribution bill that is before the House. However, I hope the commission will be able to continue its work and that when the 18 months are up and we are presented with a new formula, it will be based on the philosophy of representation by population rather than on one of the anachronisms held over from the last century, namely, the senatorial rule which discriminates against such provinces as Saskatchewan and Manitoba as compared with provinces such as New Brunswick and Newfoundland. I can visualize the day when the province of Manitoba in particular may have a population twice as large as that of New Brunswick, but because of the senatorial rule both Manitoba and New Brunswick will have ten constituencies and ten members of parliament. At present, Newfoundland has a population of 522,000, and New Brunswick 634,000. There is a possibility that over the next 15 years Newfoundland may catch up with and move ahead of New Brunswick in terms of population. When they have one more person in Newfoundland than in New Brunswick, the number of seats in Newfoundland will increase from six to ten as soon as legislation is passed.
These are just a few of the injustices in the legislation that exists in this country. I think we must be careful in the new formula to recognize that our rural areas are declining and that those constituencies should perhaps be somewhat smaller. At the same time, it is important that we keep in mind the philosophy of representation by population as the guiding principle behind legislation for the creation of constituencies.
There are one or two other matters which I should like to mention. I believe that in certain areas-the huge rural areas, for example, and the northern ridings-it may be possible to provide better facilities to members of parliament to enable them to get around their constituencies more often, and perhaps better office facilities in Ottawa that would enable them to keep in better contact with their constituents, because people living in these areas deserve as much contact with their member of parliament as do people in urban ridings. I think that is another matter which the House and the committee which deals with this legislation should keep in mind as we study the new formula for the future redistribution of seats in this country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1964-65 this House dealt with a real problem, namely, how to provide equitable representation in the Canadian parliament for all Canadians. At that time a lengthy debate took place and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act came into effect. Provision was made in that act

at the time, mainly at the insistence of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), that a margin of 25 per cent rather than the proposed 15 per cent be made part of the law, thus allowing more flexibility in the drawing of constituency maps.
It was envisaged that this 25 per cent would be applied to rural areas and to certain other situations to accommodate whole communities in order to compensate somewhat for the large acreage covered by rural areas and for the difficulties of communication in them. I do not think anybody in the House would disagree with the 25 per cent differential based on those grounds. However, we subsequently allowed certain inequities to arise and today we are debating another bill which will perpetuate those inequities for a longer period of time.
Based on the law of 1964-65 we carried out a redistribution in 1967 in time for the 1968 election. The law requires that after the decennial census the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act shall come into effect. The Canadian people would then get up to date representation subject to the 25 per cent margin mentioned in section 13(c). For over eight years parliament has known of the law. For a good many years every member of the House has known, or should have known, the probable effects of this law and the fact that certain provinces would lose seats. This should, and will, take place as population patterns in Canada change.
Why do we now bring forward a bill to suspend this law and suppress redistribution at least for the time being? Why do we inquire into this question at the last minute and after the expenditure of over $1 million of the taxpayers' money? If certain regions wanted the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act repealed or changed they should have made representations two or three years ago and not waited until now. I think I can say that few politicians in the House are anxious for redistribution because people who are successful-all the members of the House have been successful-do not want to change the basis of their success, their present constituency, for an unknown quantity. We must remember that redistribution is noi accommodate politicians; it is to accommodate the people of Canada.
I can assure the House that I, no more than the others, do not wish to lose part of the constituency which I have the honour to represent and in which I have worked hard in trying to understand the problems and knowing the people better. The constituency which I presently represent, Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton, will be chopped in half. The area in which is my residence will become a new constituency, and if I subsequently have the honour to represent that territory I will have lost eight municipalities, including a town of 10,000, and five townships of good people, people whom I am beginning to know and understand, and instead will pick up an area with which I am as yet unfamiliar. However we, the politicians, cannot and should not hold up redistribution to accommodate ourselves.
Some of the provincial redistribution commissions have made their final reports to the House of Commons. Ontario's map of electoral districts has been badly butch-
July 9, 1973

ered, and I understand that Alberta's and New Brunswick's have been similarly mangled. But these commissions are supposed to be independent. It was decided by this House to formulate these independent bodies in order to take this important basis of our democratic society out of the hands of politicians so that they could not gerrymander the electoral districts in favour of themselves or of any group within this House. Now we are being asked to reverse that step and at least temporarily or in part to take from the independent commissions their right to redistribute the electoral boundaries and return that decision-making power to the politicians.
The people of Canada are entitled to redistribution and to more equitable representation as was decided by this House in 1964-65. No redistribution will be perfect, but we should not interfere with this process now. I believe this House should clear up the many inequities which exist, take under advisement any new inequities and work on those in the next decade so that we can change the law prior to the 1981 census and achieve prompt redistribution with even better results after that census.
If certain inequities take place under the present redistribution, let us settle down next year, some seven years ahead of time, and work out a better plan for an even more equitable redistribution after the 1981 census. In the future let us not wait until the last minute. Let us rethink and replan the law in plenty of time so that the next redistribution will be even more just. Surely that would be the more honest thing to do on behalf of the people of Canada than what is suggested in this bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my words this afternoon will be brief. First I would like to say that so far as I am concerned the Boundaries Commission for the province of Saskatchewan has done an excellent job of redistribution following the 1971 census. Contrary to what some hon. members have said today and some of the speeches made last Friday, that commission did make some provision for the rural ridings.
There is provision in the act for a 25 per cent leeway from the average, or from the norm or median. In Saskatchewan these figures were supposed to produce electoral boundaries which were to have a minimum population of 57,000 and a maximum of 96,000. As a result of redistribution one riding in Saskatchewan will have a population of 63,875 and another a population of 90,506. Generally speaking, the rural ridings will have smaller populations and the more urban ridings will have larger populations. In general I would like to say that the Electoral Boundaries Commission in Saskatchewan did a commendable job.
I realize that if this bill does not pass there will be a problem with certain provinces losing the number of members of parliament to which they are presently entitled. Saskatchewan is one of them. We will drop from 13 to 12 seats. However, despite this, and even though I will not be very popular in my own province, I am opposed to this bill. I do not like the fact that the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act is being suspended until such time as parliament makes other provisions or until January 1, 1975.
During the last six or seven years members of parliament were aware that this problem would crop up. They
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension knew that some areas of Canada were losing their population. This problem should have been tackled several years ago and not just now. I oppose this bill because I believe the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act that was passed in 1964-65 was an excellent piece of legislation which took the drawing of constituency boundaries out of the hands of politicians who often drew them for selfish reasons rather than for practical purposes. It took many years to get rid of gerrymandering. I feel we should not be toying now with a proposal to suspend that act for 18 months in the hope that we will come up with some solutions during that time. Personally, I do not think that we will: it will take us a lot longer than 18 months to find solutions.
There are a number of anomalies connected with redistribution. A committee of parliament or some other body should be looking into these anomalies over the next several years. For example, according to the Canada Year Book the province of Newfoundland had a population of 522,104 in 1971, and New Brunswick a population of 634,557. New Brunswick is governed by a floor of ten members of parliament and cannot drop below that number. Newfoundland has a floor of six, and it will drop from seven to six seats under the present redistribution. I know that the population of Newfoundland is growing faster than the population of New Brunswick. Someday Newfoundland will reach the population of New Brunswick, and under the law there is the anomaly that when it does it will automatically have ten members of parliament because the law provides that where a province has a floor of ten, the representation of a province with a larger population cannot go below the floor. These are the kinds of problems that I believe will not be solved in 18 months. Neither do I think we will solve any problems by increasing the membership of this House to 299 or 300.
Certainly I think some changes should be made in our laws or the constitution to take into account representation by population, which is basic in a democratic society, and also to take into account geographic areas. Some members of parliament have been saying that it is almost impossible for them to represent constituents adequately because of the vast size and great distances associated with their constituencies. Mr. Speaker, today we have a pretty good mail service. We have telephones, television and radio. We can commuricate with our constituents far more readily than we could 25 or 30 years ago. I do not think it is as great a problem as some people represent.
I believe that the present electoral boundaries should be completed. In the event of an election being called within the next few months, of course we would have to go with the old boundaries, and I agree that there are problems in appointing returning officers, and so forth. What I do not like about this bill, however, is the suspension of the work of the commission. When the 18-month period expires, if there are no changes made in this House a new commission will be instituted and will start drawing boundaries after a few million dollars have been spent in drawing them in the first place.
On that basis, I cannot support the present bill. I think the Boundaries Commission in Saskatchewan did an eminently worth-while job. I agree with the previous speaker

July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension that we should be looking for a solution to this whole question of representation in the various provinces over the next five or six years, and should not wait until redistribution is upon us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to present my case as a rural member of parliament and support this bill. I know that those living in rural areas have an entirely different point of view of this bill from those living in heavily populated areas. I have read the reports of speeches and have heard some of the speeches made with respect to Bill C-208. I should like particularly to comment on the speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), who, as he is wont to say jokingly, represents the rural riding of Mississauga, a very small area with close to 200,000 people
100,000	of them being voters. His speech almost brought tears to my eyes when he emphasized "one man one vote" and the fact that we represent people, not acres or square miles. Those of us who are from rural ridings are aware that we represent people-people scattered over a great area, people who are difficult to contact and difficult to see personally in order to discuss their problems.
The hon. member went on to say that many members who are opposed to the new boundaries are worried about our seats. I would point out to him and others who represent city ridings that in all probability rural members are much safer in their seats than a great many of the so-called city slickers.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext:
Those of us who represent rural ridings know our people personally. Furthermore, the voters are the same year after year because the population does not move from place to place as it does in a city riding. A good many of my colleagues who represent urban ridings have informed me that when electioneering, those who have served as members of parliament for some time find when they go into the big apartment buildings that the tenants are entirely different.
Mr. Speaker, a member of parliament must wear many hats. He or she must sit in the House of Commons, listen to and take part in debates, look after correspondence, check and look after the many problems of constituents such as unemployment insurance complaints, pensions, passports, immigration, LIP grants, Opportunities for Youth grants-I could go on and on. Constituents in rural ridings consider it a duty of the member of parliament to attend the various activities that occur the year-round, such as winter and summer carnivals, the opening of community centres and publics buildings; and there are quite often more than one in a day. Many rural ridings have fall fairs and other activities, and invite the member to be in attendance. In my own riding with its present boundaries, I will be attending 15 or 16 fall fairs in August and September. These are events which I am delighted to attend, and I know a great many of the rural members feel the same way. Those of us who represent rural ridings have problems to solve or look after which urban members do not even consider. Just to name a few-docks, post offices, problems with the railways such as railway lines being abandoned and stations closed down. Many of our

ridings have Indian constituents and Indian reservations with problems that we have to solve.
The Boundaries Commission has added at least 25 per cent to my riding. The former member, Mr. Gordon Aiken, informed me that Parry Sound-Muskoka was the largest riding to service because there are people in every corner of it. Some hon. members might take exception to this statement, but after electioneering last September and October and going to every corner of it-I see some hon. members shaking their heads; I know they represent areas of many more square miles and I sympathize with them-I can confirm his statement.
It seems now that at least 25 per cent is being added if the new electoral boundaries are to be approved. It has been suggested that the county of Haliburton be included, with some 2,000 square miles and, I believe, 10,000 people. I see the hon. member for Renfrew North-Nipissing East (Mr. Hopkins) smiling. I believe I am to be offered some 20 or 30 townships in Nipissing which he represents at the present time. As far as serving as the member of parliament for these additional people is concerned, that is fine. But how much can one man look after and at the same time do a good job? I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, what they are doing to your own riding but I assume something will be done there. You are in the unfortunate position of not being able to speak out and make comments on it.
Many urban members of parliament look after a great many people. I have spoken at various times about the size of city ridings-maybe 20 blocks by 30 blocks. Even the most unhealthy city member could probably walk across his riding in an hour and a half, and those who are not too healthy would perhaps take two hours. But those of us in rural ridings have a lot of territory to cover and many problems to try to solve.
One other matter that I think can be verified is that city people do not take advantage of their voting right as much as country people do. I know there was a good vote at the last election, but time and again city voters do not turn out as well as do the voters in rural Ontario. Therefore, I do not think they are entitled to the same consideration. In my riding 76.9 per cent of the voters turned out at the last election. I know that certain city ridings had a fairly good turnout, but some did not.
There is one other point that I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members, particularly those from metropolitan Toronto, and I assume it probably applies to Montreal as well. Their populations shrink considerably during the summer months as a good many of their voters head north to cottages and resort areas. This includes a great many members of parliament who have summer cottages in my riding. A recent survey made for the district of Muskoka, which is part of my riding, shows that 13,400 private cottages are used by 72,000 people. These people make good use of their cottages on almost every weekend during the summer. This is more than the permanent population of my riding, Mr. Speaker, and does not include the many hotels, motels and resorts which comprise over 6,000 units and for which could be estimated a minimum of 10,000 people. Add to this another 50,000 campers who use the provincial camps. I am speaking only of Muskoka now, because the district of Parry Sound is a great deal larger than Muskoka and while it does not have
July 9, 1973

as many private cottages it has a great number of resorts and campsites.
These thousands of summer residents are welcome to our vacation paradise, Mr. Speaker, but I think it will be agreed that with the great increase in population the many services under federal jurisdiction are increased correspondingly. Many of these people are now working much shorter hours, and in a very few years they will have more leisure and less working time and will be extending their stay in these summer homes. With rapid transit facilities increasing, in all probability they could be classed as residents of Parry Sound-Muskoka. We could end up with the population of Toronto being decreased and ours being increased considerably.
I am aware of those provinces which will be hard hit. Members are looking very unhappily at the great province of Ontario in which my constituency is located. It should be looked at in two ways, on the basis of southern Ontario and northern Ontario. Northern Ontario will lose two seats, and southern Ontario will gain five. The province will have a net gain of three seats. Hon. members from northern Ontario will certainly react against this. They have done a good job of looking after their constituencies, which are now large engough if not too large. I hope the commissioners will give consideration to this problem. Those of us in rural parts of Canada feel we have as much as we can properly look after. I am aware of what has been stated here, namely that this pure democracy-one man, one vote. We might as well go the other way and have so many votes per square mile. Some city constituencies would not come off too well if the equation were worked both ways. This is why special consideration must be given to rural Canada and the members who represent it.
When speaking some weeks ago on the housing bill I mentioned that everything was oriented to the cities. We seem to be forgotten about. At that time I stated the the map of Canada would probably be redrawn; the ten provinces would be thrown out and there would be new provinces of Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Calgary and probably one other. The rest of us would be out in the bush. We know about the discrimination in the city compared to the rural areas as outlined by members representing urban constituencies. However, it is the people in rural Canada who have been fattening the city people. We do all our buying in the cities which are the centre of everything. The rest of us are more or less left out. On the present basis of representation, maybe we will at least get back part of what should be ours.
I feel there should be a free vote on this question. There are many members on the government side who feel the same way. They do not want the rural ridings decreased or enlarged. We believe members representing city constituencies should be able to handle many more people because they do not have the same problems.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words with regard to this bill before us. I congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) on his argument. I feel it could be supported by all members who represent rural areas. The attitude of the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick)
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension was very surprising. The area he represents is not a city constituency it is a rural constituency. He talked about gerrymandering and the like; that was surprising. Obviously, he is against the bill because the parts of his constituency that are being removed are the Liberal areas. He would be keeping a Tory constituency. It is surprising he would express that point of view.
I am a little concerned about the use of the word "gerrymandering". It is as though there were something unclean or uncouth about politicians doing the work of politicians. Who knows more about politics than politicians? It is like handing medical matters to somebody who is not a doctor. Who knows more about dividing our areas and the intimate considerations of our constituencies than members of parliament? Yet there are people who throw around the word "gerrymandering" as if there were something clandestine or something to be gained by a politician speaking in favour of or against the redistribution of seats in Canada. This is ridiculous. The ones best qualified are those who sit in this House. We know the problems, both socioeconomic and geographic. With regard to northern Ontario, it is obvious that those who are trying to make the decision with regard to dividing the constituencies have never even travelled in the area. They do not know anything about the area.
When listening to the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) the other day, I was amazed. He is a typical Toronto member who expresses a typical Toronto attitude. Toronto runs the province of Ontario. Now they want to run Ottawa as well. They would like all the members to be from Toronto. This is as unbelievable as the commission that was appointed and the commissioners who drew this map. Some months ago the commissioners made a proposal. They drew an initial map. They took away two seats from northern Ontario, leaving ten. We objected to that and made an appearance before them. When the commission was in Ottawa, several of us made representations on the basis of the socioeconomic conditions and the vast geography of northern Ontario. The commission ignored them entirely. Not only that, but at a hearing in North Bay the commissioners told our people that the members from northern Ontario, even though we had to be here for an important vote in the House that day, were disinterested and had not even bothered to come and present their views.
It is unbelievable that a justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario would go before our people in North Bay and say we were not interested enough to present our views. Almost every one of us went to the courthouse in Ottawa and made our views known. We stated what we thought should be done in the north. We pointed out that the divisions were not based on logic and did not take into consideration the facts of life. For example, we pointed out they were trying to block off an area known as Hearst which is French-speaking. They were including Hearst in an English-speaking area, leaving where that town does all of its business separated from it. We pointed that out to them, as well as a number of other things.
Because we drew to the attention of the people that the commission knew nothing about northern Ontario, had never been there and were not concerned about our basic interests, they were so upset they drew up another map

July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension which was entirely ridiculous. It was so unbelievable it is hardly worth consideration. Most of what is now the Cochcrane constituency is to be the proposed Albany-Nipigon riding. It would extend from the Quebec border to the Manitoba border. That is ridiculous. I have not measured it but it is a distance of 600, 700 or 800 miles. As anyone who has been in northern Ontario knows, there are differences between northwestern Ontario and northeastern Ontario. They also created another constituency to be known as Cochrane-Timiskaming. The only reason it bears the name Cochrane is that it includes the town of Cochrane.
The whole district of Cochrane has been thrust in elsewhere. They have made a little hump around Cochrane in such a way as to isolate the town from its traditional lines, together with such places as Smooth Rock, Kapuskasing and Hearst. It is utterly unbelievable. This is the reason, it seems to me, we must support the bill before the House and get rid of this effort which has resulted in so much criticism from Ontario and, as far as I can see, from other provinces which are equally unhappy about the way in which things have been done.
I can understand that in British Columbia people would say; "We are getting more seats, so we would like this proposal to go ahead." But the measure before us, if passed, does not mean they will not get more seats in any revised system or redistribution. Their population has increased and they will, of course, get more representation. So they need have no fear on that score. It is simply a question of extending the time so that we may have an opportunity to come up with something better than is before us now. And it will not be difficult.
Finally, I should like to say this: representation by population is a great theory. It is a great principle in certain countries. But it is not a principle which can be applied in Canada and it is time we recognized this fact. We cannot act strictly in accordance with the idea of representation by population. If we do, we shall find there are territories which cannot possibly cope with the results. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka mentioned fall fairs. There is no sitting member from Toronto who understands what it is to deal with 20 different municipalities, 20 different municipal councils.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SUSPEND OPERATION OF ACT
speechtext: Right on.

speechtext:
This is what we are faced with in our areas. Then again, we are engaged in a more personal kind of politics. In the cities most of the electors do not even know who their member is. But in our ridings they do, and they expect their member to deal with them on a more personal basis. It matters much more to people in Kapuskasing, for example, that they should be able to deal directly with their federal member than it does to someone in Toronto who is probably in contact anyway with various government offices. These are considerations which should be kept in mind. It is not a question taking anything away from anybody; it is a question of providing equitable representation in the House of Commons to people throughout the country. That is why I urge all members to support the bill so we can get these crazy

maps out of the way and come up with something better in the next 18 months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the issue of re-arranging the electoral map first arose, after the 1971 census, many protests have been heard from all sides, which shows that the method used is undoubtedly not the best.
It is not a very difficult task to calculate the number of electors in a particular region and then to fix the boundaries of ridings so that they contain 70,000 or 80,000 electors. The important thing is to bear in mind the geographical location and the distances and not to forget the services to which electors must, none the less, be entitled, such as being able to meet their member and to make the representations they think appropriate at the opportune moment. It is the act which authorizes a commission to act in this way that should be amended, so that it can better meet present needs. Various suggestions have been made, among them one concerning the number of members. This suggestion deserves to be studied. It would undoubtedly be possible to improve this situation.
The bill being debated is aimed at suspending the operation of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act. This delay will, I hope, make it possible to improve the situation. Why do we not amend the act so that this problem of representation can be solved to the best advantage?
Section 3 of the bill before us reads as follows and I quote:
An electoral boundaries commission established pursuant to section 4 of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act following the decennial census of Canada in 1971 is discharged of its duties and ceases to exist thirty days after it transmits its completed report to the Representation Commissioner as required under section 18 of the .. .
This means that the work of the commission is suspended and the Kamouraska constituency electors are quite happy about it because when someone suggested eliminating the Kamouraska constituency from the federal election map I received representations from various groups which have been in existence for many years in a constituency where parishes have commemorated their tercentenary last year, two years ago and again this year.
During a regular session of the new Chamber of Commerce of La Pocatiere, they expressed their concern about the attitude adopted by the authorities and about the implication of a readjustment of federal electoral boundaries.
The general assembly proposed that the Federation des jeunes Chambres du Canada franQais take a stand in connection with the new federal election constituencies and the reduction of Quebec representation in Parliament.
The mayors of various municipalities of the area have held several meetings. In fact, when I attended ont of those meetings they prepared a brief which I would like to quote partly so that this House will know the attitude of the officials of each municipality. This is from a brief prepared during a meeting of the Kamouraska council and I quote:
.. . during the regular session of the Kamouraska county council, held December 13, 1972, the mayors were apprised of the threaten-
July 9, 1973

ing elimination of the county through its division in two sections, one of which would be annexed to the Bellechasse county and the other to the Lower St. Lawrence county.
. . . the mayors were unanimous in protesting vigorously and set up a special committee to defend the interests of the people before the "federal electoral boundaries readjustment commission" . . .
. . . the conditions set out to appear before the Chevalier Commission did not allow the people affected by that redistribution of federal electoral boundaries to be heard easily. Maybe that commission abides by the rules of democracy but the fact still remains that only a few privileged will have had access to it, particularly in the Gaspe region and Lower St. Lawrence.
. . . the riding of Kamouraska whose name is of Indian origin and dates back to 1674 when Governor Frontenac awarded that seigneury of Kamouraska to Louis-Olivier Morel de La Durantaye, and settlers arrived there in 1695.
The riding of Kamouraska since the Confederation of 1867-
It is true that at that time the results of elections were not known because of rather orthodox election methods which already existed, and I continue to quote:
-the riding of Kamouraska-had 31 federal general elections and which allowed illustrious men like the Pelletiers, the Carrols, the Lapointes, the Steins, the Marquises and others to reach the heights of politics and the judiciary.
.. . the riding of Kamouraska which forms a well structured geographical entity with its chief town in St-Pascal, a classical college at Sainte-Anne de-la Pocatiere which has a long established reputation, the Chapais House in Saint-Denis, the novel by Anne Hebert from which the movie "Kamouraska" was produced-
-of course, the chairman of the commission perhaps had not seen the movie "Kamouraska" at that time-
-a whole history dating back many centuries that the people cannot renounce by accepting the disappearance of the name of Kamouraska.
So I think I have pointed out quite clearly that the voters of Kamouraska want to keep the name of their riding which has an historic past of which they are proud, and I am pleased to represent the voters of that riding since they decided to entrust with me the great responsibility of representing them in the parliament of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to speak at length in this debate as I know other members are anxious to express their views. However, I think I should say, as a member from the province of British Columbia, which under the present readjustment procedure expects to gain three seats, that I look upon the bill before us with very grave doubts. I recognize that there are problems under the present Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, and some hon. members have eloquently spoken about these problems; but as a member from the province of British Columbia I am anxious to see the present increase of three seats, from 23 to 26, which will take place under the readjustment proposal.
As I said a moment ago, I am conscious of the fact that there are problems in relation to the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act to which some hon. members have referred. However, with respect, I suggest to all hon. members that these problems are largely regional. It seems to me there is no particular reason this House could not pass legislation which takes into account these regional
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension difficulties without necessarily at this time postponing indefinitely, or for at least 18 months or longer, the certainty of three new seats for the province of British Columbia. I think when I say this I should point out that if I was looking at the question from a completely personal point of view I would be very much in favour of this bill because it would be to my personal advantage, as a politician, to run within the boundaries of the riding as they were on October 30, 1972.
My riding stands to be changed very substantially as a result of redistribution and, in consequence, I will be losing part of the neighbourhood in which I grew up. I will be losing from my riding a substantial part of Vancouver South where I have campaigned, not just in the one election when I was fortunate enough to be successful in that I was elected, but as well in the previous election. Therefore, I will be losing, as I think other hon. members will, a substantial area because of redistribution and the support of people I have, hopefully, represented with diligence during the last half a year or so. This will create problems because one might always expect or hope that these people will be supporters in another election.
From a personal point of view, everything would impel me to vote for this bill. I think my fundamental duty, coming from the province of British Columbia-which ought to have an increase in the number of seats-is to keep the interests of my province and its voters in mind, and that must overrule any particular preference I might have.
I think it is probably fair to say, coming from an urban area, that I agree with hon. members who have said that if you have too much adherence to the principle of representation by population this country will become lopsided, in a geographical sense, in a very severe way. While it is all very well to say we do not represent acres, trees, mountain ranges, lakes, meadows or prairies, those parts of our country have to be cared for and they must have someone speaking for them. That part of the country which becomes the hinterland as more and more people move into the city is none the less very important to us.
I recognize that we must find some accommodation between the principle of representation by population and the problems properly put before this House by hon. members who represent rural ridings who are finding it increasingly difficult, if not impossible, to properly represent vast geographic areas. Because I recognize there are problems which must be solved, I say to all hon. members I am prepared to support this bill in its reference to the committee; but I will not be prepared to support it on third reading unless there is an amendment which will, while looking after the needs of ridings that require special attention, assure the province of British Columbia of the 26 seats it ought to have now. I hope that with the help of colleagues in all parties I will be able to move an amendment so that the parts of this bill which are necessary can go ahead, but at the same time retain for my province the additional seats which the present readjustment will give it.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I might say that I was spurred on to make a few comments on behalf of my constituency by the comments

July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension a few minutes ago of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart).

speechtext: Do you know where that is?

speechtext:
Yes, I do; I had the good fortune-and I wish more of the young people in our cities could do likewise-of travelling in northern Ontario. I not only enjoyed the natural wilderness but I also saw the mining towns, met the people and saw the problems peculiar to those areas.
It was mentioned a few moments ago that one of the problems in the city results from the fact that there are so many conglomerates and so much activity that the people do not know the borders of their ridings and in some cases do not even know who is their member of parliament. I realize that as metropolitan areas increase in size, this confusion also increases and creates an even greater disparity between urban and rural ridings.
If the problem in rural Canada is related to distance and geography, I suggest one of the greatest problems in an urban riding results from the number of municipalities which exist in such an area. This results in almost hopeless confusion for the representative. One finds great difficulty in deciding who is responsible for various things, who, and what level of government one should approach to find a solution, and so on. The hon. member for Cochrane said that urban representatives realize the problems which are inherent to those who have many municipalities within their constituencies. I certainly know the problem, because if I don't have 20, I do have three within my constituency. My people are confused, not only about their federal riding but also about the municipal area and questions such as which is Rexdale, which is Etobicoke versus Rexdale, what is North York compared to Downsview, and what is Weston compared to York and Mount Dennis. There are all those problems and confusions.
There is also lack of the spirit of a particular community which I believe many of our rural areas have been able to maintain. There is lack of the friendliness of rural Canada where one knows his neighbours and where roots are set down. The people of my area who are confused are not from Toronto, if you go back in time, but are from Cochrane, from western Canada, from northern Quebec, from the Maritimes, from Italy, from Germany or from Great Britain. There is great confusion involved in getting to know one another. There is confusion of knowing who to go to.
This confusion is added to when there is the problem of redistribution. My riding, according to the latest recut of the map, is split entirely differently from the way it was split a month or two ago. This is the result of the representations I made to the Ontario division of the redistribution commission. The commission saw fit to take my advice to the effect that my area had been cut up improperly. However, the members of the commission did not find my solutions correct. They brought in their own solutions. When I looked at their solutions and their wisdom, I must admit that they have done something I believe is better than the suggestion I had already made to them. They managed to develop the riding so that in fact one does

represent Rexdale only, and another new riding represents a portion of Etobicoke and does not wander into another municipality.
They did, indeed, separate the North York portion from the York portion and took a divided community that has been established for many years which was enveloped by suburban growth, Weston, and in fact put it into one area which will become York South Weston, and I think handed over to the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) a very sound riding for his particular political philosophy.
It has been done in this way, and if this particular redistribution were to go through I would hope this would not change again in eight or ten years hence and that the planning would start to be done within the urban areas to take into consideration the needs of the various pockets within suburbia or within the city core, because we have pockets or communities every bit as much as rural Canada has.
I support this bill because I believe in the principle of representation by population, but also I very much respect and am very well aware of the problems faced by our rural representatives. There are the distances involved as much as there are the benefits of neighourliness or lack of confusion and confrontation because of roots having been put down. There are established municipalities which are understood by rural voters. Some of these benefits are lost by the redistribution. In turn in urban areas it happens when we are trying to build the community that first steps are lost by this act of redistribution. Yet you come back to representation by population, and I believe in it.
I hope this bill will pass and that in time we will find a solution that would guarantee in our cities an identifiable base, would guarantee no further erosion for rural Canada and also would give us within the suburban areas a chance to establish an identity as a political area no matter what party is involved, an area where people can understand what it is, can seek assistance directly and can understand who the member of parliament is and where the boundaries are. In that way we could be more effective and the constituents could better understand the role of the federal level of politics. So I support this bill, not because I do not believe in representation by population-it must be continued-but because I believe if we are to give representation by population we must also protect our rural communities.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to enter this debate, but I was moved somewhat by the speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart) a few moments ago. He and I from time to time have disagreed with regard to various things we have discussed in the House. However, it has always been the friendliest kind of disagreement. I believe we understood each other on those points. Today I am pleased to be able to stand in the House and say I listened to his speech with great enjoyment. I understood the points he was trying to make. I might say that originally I came from a small town on the St. Lawrence River and therefore understand the difficulties involved and the feelings that people sometimes have in these areas because of disorientation. I say to him that I enjoyed his speech
July 9, 1973

which was delivered with clarity and in an articulate manner.
I, for one, commend the commission in the province of Ontario for the work it did. When I appeared before the commission it was the first opportunity I had had to appear before a commission of this nature, although I had listened to hearings earlier when a professional colleague of mine appeared before the commission. At that time I remember the very articulate arguments put forward by the hon. Joe Green, now a member of the Senate, and hon. Richard Bell, now a practising lawyer in the city of Ottawa. They were both members of this House.
On the occasion of my appearance before ths commission I was struck with the kindness and the attentiveness which the commission directed to the members who appeared before them. I am satisfied that all the representations made to that commission have not been of a political nature. I am satisfied that members who expressed various points of view were in fact expressing the points of view of the areas they represent.
In this debate we have heard what I might call the absolute rural viewpoint and the absolute urban viewpoint. I do not know whether it is possible to reconcile the two. None the less, it is the work of the commission to reconcile them if the commission is to function. I support the bill because I think we must consider a number of factors in the course of redistribution. I, frankly, agree with the hon. member for Cochrane when he says there is a place for politicians in this, the essence of the political process, the bedrock of the political process in Canada, namely, the delineation of the boundaries of constituencies.
Whether the politician is a member of this House, an aspirant to this House or a former member of this House, there is a place for all the collective wisdom of those politicians. I believe that this bill will give that kind of opportunity for the political side to actually intervene in the process as something more than merely counsel for a particular cause. In that regard, the so-called foisting of the resolution is a good move on the government's part and I support it.
Secondly, I want to say that my area is perhaps an amalgam of extremes. In the northern part of the riding there is a very highly concentrated area which is either blessed or plagued, depending on your point of view, with people being stacked one on top of the other in high-rise buildings. It is suffering from the whole problem of transportation and is concerned with the question of housing. It has all the problems of a highly concentrated urban area. Toward the middle of the riding and into the southern part there is a very strong agricultural belt which feels itself somewhat ignored. At the south end there is the St. Lawrence Seaway system with the small towns and villages in that area. Throughout the whole area there are different interests.
I feel that if I have any quarrel with the commission, it is that perhaps it has looked too much at the numerical side of things in the report, in terms of merely representation by population, and has not looked hard enough at some of the social, economic and sociological pulls which keep a community together, bring a community together and preserve it and the traditions which go with it. Some
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension people say we should cast off some of these traditions. In my respectful submission, Mr. Speaker, our traditions are extremely important, even the local ones, and they ought to be considered. For instance, there is a proposal that the historic village of Richmond be removed from a riding that is associated directly with the national capital. In respect of my riding, it calls for a place such as Stittsville to be removed from that orbit. It calls for a township such as Goulbourn to be moved out of the orbit of the national capital where the county council to which those municipalities owed their allegiance had its county seat. Some say that this is not really important, but out of that early, sound, local government tradition developed the economic base, and Richmond, Stittsville and the developing area of Goulbourn are now becoming the dormitories for people who work in the national capital and for many of those who look to the federal government for employment.
Those are considerations which the commission, perhaps by its terms of reference, cannot take into account as well as can a person who is interested in public life, whether that person is a member of the House or otherwise. This is why I say that the point made by the hon. member for Cochrane is important. You have to consider the limbo land, so to speak, between the north and south of a riding such as mine. What happens to the town of Kemptville? Is there a geographical pull to Ottawa, or is the pull to the city of Brockville where the representation commissioners would like to put it? This is part of that tradition as well. We must remember it. I think it is important that these traditions not be forgotten.
I do not want to fault the commission completely, because it did listen to what I at least consider to be a very important representation with respect to the location of the new ridings as proposed. I said to the commission that they should preserve, in part of what is now the constituency of Grenville-Carleton, the name Carleton since it has such a long and distinguished history which goes back to the time of the dissolution of the district of Bathurst. The commission did see fit to recognize that name and call the riding, in part, Carleton.
They also recognized the fact that the great, growing area in part of the riding taken out of Grenville-Carleton by this redistribution bill is situated in the municipality of Nepean which, despite the boasts of some of my colleagues from Toronto, Montreal and other places, is perhaps one of the fastest growing and most municipally conscious municipalities in the province of Ontario. As a result, the new riding proposed to encompass part of it is called the riding of Carleton-Nepean. I would rather have had the names reversed because the words flow together a little better, but I am quite happy that this important tradition, the old and the new, has been recognized by the commission.
The importance of this bill is that it will give all members of the House and those who are interested in the future of the House an opportunity at least to go again before a committee of the House, I hope, and advance views as to why tradition should be recognized and why the very important social, economic and other pulls should be recognized.

July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
One further reason is perhaps peculiar to any constituency that intrudes upon or is part of the national capital area. In the province of Ontario, for better or for worse, the local municipalities which make up the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton-which is the first region in the province of Ontario-are now going through their own traumatic problems of amalgamation. As a result of this there has been a certain unsteadiness, a feeling of instability and of impending change that has come about in the political process, albeit related to the other political process in which we in the House have the honour to participate.
I believe that by delaying at least another form of political upheaval we will accomplish some form of stability while another jurisdiction worries about the form which the local government, the very bedrock of government, shall take, and that we will not be contributing to further instability and possible fears of change and disorientation. As the last speaker mentioned, the importance of maintaining orientation cannot be overemphasized.
For that reason I am very pleased to support this bill. I suppose I can be forgiven if I say that I also have a selfish reason for wanting to support it. My constituency is varied and interesting. I told my colleagues, through you, Sir, about the variety of life in the community and the honour it is to represent it; but more than that, let me say that in my particular situation I have the honour to represent the area in which I was born and raised, where my children go to school and where my parents live, as well as the area from which my family sprang. I suppose there are some members in the House who in a society which has become mobile have that opportunity, but I dare say there are few indeed.
Frankly and quite honestly-I hope this remark will not be misinterpreted-I enjoy representing this seat, with the background I have in it. I want to see this area preserved for that very selfish reason. I ask my colleagues, through you, Mr. Speaker, to give weight to the remarks I have made on this bill, especially with regard to the first items which I mentioned which are extremely important. I am very pleased today to have the opportunity to support the general submissions made by my colleague, the hon. member for Cochrane.
