speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to make a few comments about the bill now before us in order to express in this House the wish of the people from the riding of Bellechasse as regards the amendment of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act.
The boundaries of the electoral district of Bellechasse were substantially changed in 1965, as a result of the electoral map redistribution. During that same year, parliament had passed a legislation that assigned to independant commissions, in each province, the responsibility for the readjustment of the representation in the House of Commons.
The Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act provides, and I quote:
For the decennial census taken in the year 1961 and for each decennial census taken thereafter, ten commissions shall be estab-

lished in the manner provided in this Act, to consider and report upon the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons required to be made upon the completion of such census.
The act states strict and specific rules that govern the division of provinces in electoral districts and the establishment of their boundaries. The first rule provides that the population of each electoral district in a province must correspond as nearly as may be to the electoral quota for the province.
And the electoral quota of a province is obtained by dividing the population of the province as ascertained by the census by the number of members of the House of Commons to be assigned to the province.
The act also states that it is possible to depart from the strict application of this rule if special geographic considerations, including in particular the sparsity, density or relative rate of growth of population of various regions of the province, the accessibility of such regions or the size or shape thereof, appear to the commission to render such a departure necessary.
Is short, Mr. Speaker, in each province the commission was responsible for the electoral boundaries readjustment and for compliance with the regulations enacted by the law. I think it is a question of mathematics and the commissioners did not have to sit for weeks to make this redistribution. I consider that grade 12 students were able to compute the census figures and to make the division to try to adjust rural parishes and to try as much as possible to comply with the standards enacted by the law.
Then the revision of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and the readjustment of the electoral map in 1965 were made from the 1961 census data. According to these data, the electoral quota of the province of Quebec was established at 71,070.
Taking into account the margin of 25 per cent under and over the electoral quota, acceptable limits were from 53,303 to 88,837 people. According to the first representation order made in 1952, the riding of Bellechasse had 32,513 people in 1961.
In 1968, after the revision, the new riding of Bellechasse included 69,075 people. According to the law, the new boundary commission for Quebec was established after the last census in order to inquire and to report on the readjustment of the representation of the province in the House of Commons.
The new electoral quota for the province has been set at 83,719 inhabitants per constituency. Taking into consideration the allowable margin of 25 per cent under and above that quota, the limits are therefore 62,798 or 104,649. As a rule, according to the 1971 statistics, the Bellechasse constituency remains within the limits of the allowable minimum margin.
However, the Electoral Boundaries Commission has suggested new boundaries for the Bellechasse constituency. Under that new proposal, the entire area of the Lower St. Lawrence between Quebec City and Riviere-du-Loup is substantially altered as a result of the abolition of the Kamouraska constituency.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I support the comments made a few minutes ago by the hon. member for
July 9, 1973

Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) about the review of that legislation. The hon. member for Kamouraska was quite right in letting the House know the reasons why the public organizations of Kamouraska objected to the disappearance of this historical riding.
This is also why I support his remarks wholeheartedly, because by removing the electoral district of Kamouraska, another rural riding is going to vanish and we will have one member less in the House of Commons, and goodness knows that the people in rural ridings need more than ever, their representatives in assemblies like this parliament, in order to let their situation be known and obtain as much help as possible for the development of their sector.
As I said a moment ago, the electoral map has greatly upset the area I have the honour to represent. Prior to 1968, there were three members: one representative for the electoral district of Dorchester, another for the electoral district of Bellechasse and a third for the electoral district of Montmagny. After the readjustment of the electoral boundaries, all this territory was entrusted to only one member, therefore, two rural ridings were automatically eliminated. The Dorchester and Montmagny constituents felt somewhat frustrated because the names of their constituencies had been dropped.
Mr. Speaker, this is quite normal: there were three names for only one territory. There were consultations between the commission and some people and, finally, the name Bellechasse was retained; nevertheless, the voters from what used to be the Dorchester constituency were used to the name Dorchester, which had a past, for this constituency was quite historical; as to the Montmagny constituency, the change created something of a schism.
Those who took part in the 1968 election campaign had to be very tactful not to make matters worse with words and names, but to try and make the people understand that it had been done with the best intentions, even though it did not appear quite acceptable to them.
Mr. Speaker, I consider that some principles should orient any changes in the representation, the first one being-and I insist on this-that between changes in the representation, the electoral boundary readjustments should be limited to the absolute minimum.
Human beings are slaves to their habits and radical transformations of electoral districts should be avoided as much as possible. To this end, I think that every effort should be made toward relative permanency, that boundaries should be so set that an increasing population could readily adapt to them and also, aim at making the least possible changes necessary. That is a must, particularly if we want to ensure appropriate and stable political parties.
The proposed distribution departs substantially from provincial boundaries. It is again a thorough change that gives rise to certain problems such as those we had last fall, for example, when help was provided for farmers whose harvest had been damaged by frequent rainfalls. So a conflict arose that is not yet entirely resolved precisely because of those differences between federal and provincial electoral boundaries.
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
The main factor to be considered to have truly representative members in the House of Commons is cultural, social and economic homogeneity between ridings, which rural members really insist on. I cannot blame them for it, I am a rural member myself, and I understand perfectly their feelings. That is why I want to express to the House the feelings of those people so greater consideration will be given to those ideas when the government decides within the period set out in the act to revise the act, to introduce amendments or even write a new act that will be more consistent with the aspirations of the people.
For my part, I consulted a number of my follow citizens in the riding of Bellechasse as well as many others and most of them are very aware of the important factor of cultural, geographical, economic and social entity and unity.
Mr. Speaker, may I be also permitted to emphasize again the utmost importance of the difference between rural and urban ridings. In my years as a member I noted on several occasions that rural members are overloaded in comparison with urban members. Let me explain: I do not mean by that that urban members have no work; that is not it at all. I mean that comparatively-and I am going to explain it a little more later-the representatives of rural ridings, because of the sheer area, must necessarily give much more time to their duties. Indeed, since the last revision of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, rural ridings have been expanded, which requires the member to travel miles and miles every weekend in order to keep in contact with the people he represents. And this contact has become more and more necessary if you expect the member to make the required representations in full knowledge and in due time.
The member of parliament must be present not only politically, but also on the social and economic planes. This is why we must reckon with this factor. It is much easier, in my view, to represent 80,000 people concentrated in a city than 60,000 people scattered through a huge rural territory.
Consideration must also be given to the fact that the member who represents a rural riding travels at his own expense within its limits, at rather considerable expenses. That is why we insist-and I congratulate the hon. members who brought up the matter during this debate-that the government should decide, as soon as possible, to help with setting up an office in every riding, with proper services, to accommodate the population. This, not to accommodate the member but the people. It would be the member's office, regardless of his political affiliation, where the people could contact their member or, through the secretaries, Ottawa. Our constituents would find it easier to get in touch with us while avoiding substantial travel expenses and saving time and hardships. I think this is a service which should be created urgently for our constituents and which would permit parliament members to discharge their duties more completely and efficiently.
Another aspect of the problem which should also be considered is the fact that rural areas are less and less populated and if we maintain the current criteria it is obvious that rural citizens will have less and less representation in this House and that the province of Quebec will also lose a few seats which would be most

July 9, 1973
Adjournment Motion
unfortunate. I object to the Quebec representation being reduced because it is one of the four provinces which participated in the foundation of the Confederation. I would be quite unhappy if, because of this act, the number of Quebec members should diminish.
I would also emphasize again that we should not overload the rural area members from the population standpoint-I would suggest between 50,000 and 60,000 people- so as not to weaken the contacts they should have with the population if our democratic system is to be reinforced. Only yesterday I saw how it was necessary for a member of parliament to be closer to the people and in a position to be in contact with them if he truly wants to be their spokesman and convey their ideas to the authorities.
I hope that in view of the time period provided for in the bill the government will have the opportunity and the time required to prepare amendments or a legislation which would truly reflect the people's aspirations, in other words a legislation which would eliminate the shortcomings of the law because if the current law was implemented it would entail new complications. In fact, several provinces other than Quebec would be frustrated. Suffice it to study the reports of the various commissions to find out how many members some provinces would lose, for instance.
I suppose, in view of the fact that our Canadian population is increasing, it is not normal that the number of representatives in this House should be reduced. For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall make a point of supporting the bill and to vote if required.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIVAL OF CANADIAN MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reviving the Canadian merchant marine.
He said: Mr. Speaker, once again I am speaking on a subject of which I have been a strong proponent since I came to this House many years ago. This subject, the revival of the Canadian merchant marine, is one of fundamental importance to me, to my home town of Saint John and to the constituency which I have the honour to represent. It is one that must be discussed if any serious and responsible approach to the problems of regional disparity in the Atlantic area is to be considered. It is a subject which must be faced in the planning of any future development in the Arctic. It is one which is of prime importance to the west coast and its expanding relationship with the Far East. Such revival will be of increasing importance as Canada plans to manage effectively its continental shelf resources. Lastly, the subject of a merchant marine is directly related to Canada's position as one of the world's great trading nations.
I want to say at the outset that I consider a merchant marine only one area of an over-all marine policy that requires immediate review. Perhaps I should clarify the term "marine policy" for those on the government benches who may, by some chance, have heard the expression but who obviously have never grasped its meaning or significance. By "marine policy" I mean a clear, concise and comprehensive policy covering not only a Canadian-owned merchant marine-and that is both coastal and deep sea-but also ship-building and repair, ports and harbours and related specialized marine educational facilities.
The Liberal government's various policies on this subject, where they exist, have always been ad hoc, hodgepodge; they have never been co-ordinating, and have often been conflicting. Although Canada possesses one of the longest coastlines in the world, government thinking has created the impression that we are as landlocked as Zambia. Yes, Mr. Speaker, as someone has said, we truly are a nation of landlubbers. At the present time Atlantic Canada continues to suffer from the highest rate of unemployment in the country-a rate which would be considered disgraceful and unacceptable in any other nation with an appreciation of social conscience.
The Atlantic region continues to see its brightest and best trained young men and women leave the area in search of employment elsewhere, leaving those who remain to face an increasingly heavy burden of taxation and the like. Federal policy-makers and advisers have apparently accepted this situation as inevitable, designing programs which at best only maintain the status quo. The gap between our region and the rest of Canada continues merrily on its way.
July 9, 1973

I am convinced that this kind of thinking stems from the conscious or unconscious acceptance of that old, simplistic and completely erroneous argument that says maritime prosperity died when the era of wooden sailing ships ended. I have never, and will never accept this argument for it implies that maritimers cannot build or sail new, modern ships. The shipyards of Saint John built the finest sailing ships of the day. The Marco Polo, for example, built by Saint John craftsmen, carried our flag to the four corners of the world as the fastest clipper ship on record.
While I was serving in the merchant marine during World War II, it was generally accepted that the finest ships' officers and the most able sailors were more often than not men raised in the outports, the fishing villages and harbours of the Atlantic provinces, clearly showing that a proud maritime tradition did not end with the passing of wooden ships.
However, it is not my intention to appeal to nostalgia but, rather, to point out the revolutionary changes in shipping which now present Canada with an unsurpassed opportunity to take advantage of these human resources of the Atlantic region. Coupled with this opportunity presented by trends in shipping is the challenge facing Canada in developing the Arctic and exploring for offshore resources, a challenge which demonstrates vividly our inadequate marine capabilities. But first may I mention the new world trends in ship characteristics. The astonishing technological developments in world shipping in the past decade in terms of size, automation and specialization have created a situation where ships built prior to 1960 are often completely obsolete when competing with newer ships of their respective trades. The most obvious of the prevailing trends in shipbuilding is the increase in size of the individual ships being built. This is certainly true with regard to the tanker and bulk carrier fleets.
A few years ago a 50,000-ton tanker was considered a giant of the trade. Today, this same sized ship is used primarily for semi-refined products in the coastal trade. In 1963 tankers of over 60,000 tons dead weight comprised only 5.2 per cent of total fleet tonnage, but by 1972, tankers of this size formed 60 per cent of the total tonnage. Of the 983 tankers on order as of April 30, 1972, about 39 per cent of the ships and 83 per cent of the tonnage was accounted for by tankers of at least 150,000 tons dead weight. Of the latter, 47 per cent of the ships and 83 per cent of the tonnage was concentrated in the 250,000 to 300,000-ton category.
There has also been a parallel increase in the average ship tonnage of the main bulk carrier types. Between the years 1960 and 1972 there was a 66 per cent increase in the average tons, dead weight, of ore carriers. During the same period the average size of combined ore or oil carriers tripled and combined bulk or oil carriers nearly quadrupled, while the average tons, dead weight, of other dry bulk carriers doubled.
However, today there appears to be stabilization of the growth in ship size. It seems we have reached a plateau in this regard, and although the economies of scale related to the bigger vessels still exist there are practical and managerial problems involved in their operation which
Canadian Merchant Marine
make large scale production of ships above 400,000 tons dead weight unlikely in the immediate future.
Along with increasing size and automation in shipping developments has come increasing specialization in function. The current trend has been away from the multipurpose or multicargo vessel and toward ships designed for and employed in the carriage of a particular commodity. The days of the tramp steamer and old Liberty ships are gone. They have given way to the container vessel, the roll-on/roll-off ship and other specialized carriers.
What does all this mean in terms of reviving the Canadian merchant marine? I feel these factors are favourable for such a revival. The period of rapid and revolutionary changes in world shipping appears to be about over and the present conditions left by these changes seem well suited for Canadian shipping needs. The 200,000 to 250,000-ton tanker and bulk or oil carrier would give us the economies of scale of the large vessels and fit in well with our import export demands on shipping, while not presenting us with any practical managerial problems. It should also be pointed out that this is most likely the best sized ship for use in the Arctic, a subject I will discuss in a moment.
The reduced crew size brought about by semi-automation should go a long way toward overcoming the old problem of higher Canadian crew costs while at the same time creating an acceptable amount of on-board employment. However, it must be noted that these on-board jobs will form the smallest percentage of the employment generated by a merchant marine. It is deceptive to only compare the number of crew jobs to the capital outlay involved in a Canadian fleet and exclude the thousands of new jobs in related repair, supply and service industries that such a fleet would bring about.
Any observer of the rapidly increasing interest in the development of the Arctic and our offshore mineral resources must be struck by the glaring inconsistencies of government policy in this area. On one hand we hear loud proclamations about our sovereignty over the Arctic and vague rumblings about extending the territorial boundary to the edge of the continental shelf, but on the other hand government landlubbers appear oblivious of the need to have Canadian vessels and crews used in the development and exploration of our resources in the north and our offshore waters. In short, we see the establishment of national goals, and yet one the most obvious vehicles for obtaining these objectives has been ignored by the government.
How can we expect other nations to take seriously our claims of the right to manage offshore resources and sovereignty of the Arctic when we possess neither the marine capability of enforcing such claims nor the vessels needed for the exploration and transshipment of these resources? More important, we have given no indication we plan to obtain this kind of capability.
We must act now to implement policies which will permit the true revival of the Canadian merchant marine-a merchant marine which will provide the vehicle for obtaining our stated national goals, a merchant marine which will generate employment in those sea-related insdustries in which we have traditionally excelled, and a merchant marine which will enable us to

July 9, 1973
Canadian Merchant Marine
play a role in the sea lanes of the world more in keeping with the proud maritime tradition of the people of both our coasts.
Please notice that I am not advocating the establishment of a merchant on the scale of Great Britain, Japan or Norway which would compete with those existing large national fleets. Rather, I favour a Canadian fleet designed and tailored to Canadian needs, a fleet which would provide the nucleus of future expansion and become a steady source of work for the on-shore repair, service and supply industries.
What exact form government assistance required for the revival of the merchant marine should take is debatable. What is not debatable is that some kind of government assistance is needed. There have been numerous studies, reports and briefs on this and related subjects-one every year at least for the last ten years. The time has come for action on these reports. In light of the non-partisan support my motion has received in the past from all quarters of the House, I propose we set up a special committee composed of members from all parties to study the proposal and make recommendations to the government as to the kinds and forms of assistance needed for the revival of a Canadian merchant fleet.
The committee would include hon. members from the St. Lawrence area who have an interest in this subject and who have been promised action on it every day of the week by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). And at election time he really makes it a big issue. Here is a great challenge for an enterprising minister of transport. We have had a lot of do-nothing ministers around for the last decade. The only one who did anything was Mr. Pickersgill. He was criticized, but at least he had an objective, a wish to do something about the railways and he went ahead and did it. The present minister should accept this challenge and recognize that something can be done. He could develop the necessary vessels required in the exploitation of our resources in the Arctic and off our coasts. It is a challenge to all concerned to use our technical knowledge, know-how and experience in this field and not let these assets be wasted. It is a challenge to the Canadian government to state firmly that these are Canadian resources and that Canadians, and only Canadians, shall utilize those resources.

speakeroldname: Mr. Raynald Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIVAL OF CANADIAN MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell), I have had several opportunities to take part in this debate concerning the merchant marine. Recently, on February 21 during my speech on the budget, I pointed out the importance of creating a Canadian merchant marine, a field in which our country has not played a part for several years although Canada's import and ^ export trade places it among the most important nations in the world.
I added that there would be tremendous benefits for our economy in view of the ever increasing quantity of goods and commodities such as seeds, oil, minerals, coal, timber

and many others that must be exported from Canada. In this field it is difficult to accept the almost complete absence of Canadian ships or ships flying the Canadian flag and I already made this a matter of national prestige.
I have not changed my mind since, quite the contrary. I become more and more aware of the need to establish a Canadian merchant marine since there is nothing so apparent as the total lack of a sea-going merchant marine.
Such a situation is most abnormal in a country which has a wealth of the expertness and industrial resources required to build and operate a merchant marine.
This gap in our commercial development affects all Canadians, whether they rely on merchant marine for access to markets or operate ships or build them as is the case for my constituents.
My interest in the matter is therefore twofold. First, as a Canadian believing in the economic need of immediately putting up a merchant marine, and afterwards as a representative of the Levis constituency and of all the workers of the shipyards for whom I am the spokesman in this House.
Right now, the situation is all the worst because Canada has a marine tradition of which it is proud.
In the years following 1867, our country was in 4th place amongst the nations which had a merchant marine. As shipbuilders, we ranked third during World War II, just behind the United States and Great Britain.
What is possible in times of war should also possible in peacetime for constructive reasons. A modern merchant marine would guarantee the expansion of our foreign trade and would actively contribute to an increase of our exports. It would provide jobs for thousands of Canadians. It would perforce bring about a technical modernization of an important sector of our heavy industry. It would provide additional income for several allied industries and various communities.
The 1970 Hedlinmenzies report considered the economic feasibility of a Canadian merchant fleet and showed that certain prototypes of ships would ensure the viability of such a fleet. I understand that bulk and container type ships would be better adapted to our needs; this is easy to prove and to comprehend if one looks, for example, at our ever-increasing exports of Canadian wheat.
With regard to the ship sizes analysed and suggested in the report, my personal conclusion would be that in view of the tough competition now going on between bulk carrier ships, Canada should think about being a leader in this field since, in any case, a one million ton bulk carrier Canadian fleet would make up only a small part of the world's fleet of such ships, or slightly under five per cent. The day of the 10,000 ton ship is gone, and when one considers those now being built in Japan, it is time to take some precautions if we want to make this a profitable enterprise.
Most of our markets are distant ones, and several years' experience have shown that the longer the voyage, the larger the ship should be. What is more, further savings can be realized through full automation, this saving on manpower. It has also been demonstrated that the heavy

tonnage cargo ship saves about 50 per cent per ton-mile on fuel.	.
Since, to all appearances, we are greatly in need of large bulk carrier ships, since we have considerable experience in ship-building, and since our shipyards, especially those in my constituency, are capable of carrying out a project of the scope suggested, it only remains for the government of Canada to enact the necessary legislation.
With reference to the notice of motion moved by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell), it is my opinion that we should immediately begin to study, prepare and adopt legislation to provide continuing assistance, by the most appropriate methods, to Canadian shipowners, seamen, shipyards and maritime workers, as well as to suppliers of materials, components and equipment; a policy of this nature would be of permanent benefit to all classes of Canadian society.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIVAL OF CANADIAN MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a lot of argument in this House on the recommendations contained in the Darling report; we have heard a lot of argument in favour of the construction of a Canadian merchant marine. After so much has been said, I believe the time for idle chatter is over. It is time for us to start planning for a Canadian merchant marine in which we can take pride. In this way we could provide ships for Canadian seamen and employment for workers in our Canadian shipyards.
We have heard in the last few months arguments for and against the Darling report. I think this report constitutes the basic requirement for future expansion of a Canadian merchant fleet. It is, therefore, with much concern that I view this whole report and its future relationship to a Canadian deep sea merchant marine. There is no doubt that politicians in the Atlantic provinces are opposed to this report on the ground that rail and water transportation rates will increase and that the economy of the Mari-times will be jeopardized as a result of such an increase. I do not buy that argument. I think there are other economic factors that must be considered in light of this report and in light of what we should be dealing with now and in the future. We have all heard of the Darling report and how Canadian ships should be allowed to ply between Canadian ports. We have heard about the resources in the Arctic and the offshore areas which in future will require the services of Canadian ships. We have listened to these and other arguments as to what should be done.
Another area about which I am concerned is the development of a Canadian shipping fleet. There is no justification in the argument that corporations such as IBM, Crown Zellerbach and others have been established, to the tune of millions of dollars, when B.C. shipyards are in need of work and help is not forthcoming. Surely British Columbia, with its high unemployment rate, requires some consideration when it comes to shipbuilding.
We have seen how the shipyards in eastern Canada have proven themselves very efficient and capable and will no doubt prove themselves capable of building more ships in the future, particularly if we pursue this policy in relation
Canadian Merchant Marine
to a Canadian deep sea merchant fleet. We have been shortsighted in the past with regard to these needs. Previous governments could have helped toward the retention of a fleet such as we had during the Second World War, but they have been very shortsighted and have given in to the interests of companies such as the Canadian Pacific, Irving of the maritimes and others who feel they can develop more through their own interests. Where the interests of people are concerned, surely Canadian interests are more important than the interests of these companies. It is time we got away from this kind of smokescreen.
We have seen how dummy corporations are set up to serve these private interests at the expense of the people of Canada. It is time the government took a dim view of the activities of these dummy corporations and did something more practical and justifiable in order that we might develop a merchant marine of which we can be proud. The merchant marine has helped a great deal toward the development of this country. We should reinstate this service in order that the young people of Canada can serve in it and see the world. They could then be part of the economic development of this vast sector of our economy.
We must be longsighted with regard to areas such as the Arctic and offshore development. We must be longsighted in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer. We have to institute a policy whereby the merchant marine can be developed. We must develop a policy through which it will be economically feasible to develop a deep sea merchant marine to serve the interests of this country. It is to this end that I have spoken on a number of occasions in this House in support of the Darling report. If we are to develop a deep sea merchant marine we must develop a policy along the lines recommended in that report. This must be an initial step.
A merchant marine along the lines I envisage will, I believe, soon become a reality. It must become a reality. But it requires interest on the part of the Canadian people and the Canadian government. I look forward to the expansion of our shipbuilding industry on the west coast and on the east coast. I look forward to increased employment in the shipping industry and other industries directly and indirectly associated with it. I have no doubt that this will become a reality, because water transportation is vital.
I therefore urge the federal government to make its position known in respect of the Darling report and to carry out an immediate study for the development of a merchant marine by the establishment of a Crown corporation to initiate such development. The government's interest in the matter is absolutely essential, and steps taken to boost this country's economy must be reflected in this interest. Only by being realistic about the needs of a growing economy and by following Australia's recent action to reserve the coastal shipping trade for Australia- building and manning vessels-can this country put itself in a more favourable position for a future thrust in the deep sea trade.
In conclusion, I hope very sincerely that the government will carry out a policy which will reflect its interest in the needs of this country, a policy to serve the needs of Canada in the future.

July 9, 1973
Canadian Merchant Marine

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIVAL OF CANADIAN MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased and honoured this afternoon to be able to second this resolution. To me, here is an opportunity to bring substance to our national motto, with the deposition of this motion by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) and my seconding it as the member for the riding of Esquimalt-Saanich. By passing the motion we would be giving meaning to our motto "A mari usque ad mare".
This also gives me an opportunity to enlarge on the theme which I began to develop during my participation in the budget debate. When I was speaking then, with the limitations in time which were imposed, I was able to deal with only two aspects of what I have called a Canadian marine services policy, those two aspects having to do with the coastguard and pollution.
The third and fourth elements of my plea for a real, live and thriving marine services policy for Canada, which I enjoin the government to adopt, are related to the merchant marine and to shipbuilding. My interests in this subject are of prime importance to shipbuilding in the area which I represent. I also have a very deep sentimental attachment to this subject because of an experience I had during the war. It was a matter of great pride for me to arrive at Port Said one sunny afternoon in late 1942 and to find I was being asked to escort the ship Princess Marguerite. This ship at one time plied between Vancouver and Victoria, and it was then a troop carrier. Unfortunately the Marguerite was later lost but I am glad to say not while I was convoying her.
I am aware of all the objections that have been levelled at the notion of a revived merchant marine for Canada. I know that many of these objections are formulated by experienced and well-meaning people. I do not question their sincerity; nor would I venture to question the lessons of the experiences they have had. In some cases, those experiences have been enough to drive the most devoted sea-dog alive from the sea and make him into a confirmed land-lubber. But this must not cause us to turn our back on our natural tradition and our national inheritance.
Canada's merchant marine, built up during the war and maintained for a time after the war's end, was not an outstanding success as a peacetime exercise. The reasons for its failure have been mentioned by some speakers, and doubtless there were many. There is no need here and now to attempt to assign blame for the failure that the CMS unquestionably was in peacetime. It really did not get off to a good start in civvy street, but let us leave it at that.
The merchant marine I envisage is not one that would be run by the Department of Transport; far from it. I want to see a privately-owned merchant fleet for the carriage of goods to and from Canadian ports and for the carriage of goods in other international trading as well. It is not my intention, even if it were within my capabilities, to describe how an effective merchant service should be run. What I intend to do is to outline some of the reasons prompting me to urge upon this House and the government to adopt policies favouring the re-creation of a Canadian merchant fleet. My purpose is to lay before this

House the reasons which make me believe in the need for a merchant fleet under a Canadian flag.
The main argument I make for a merchant fleet is that a trading nation like Canada is, and will remain, a self-made hostage to flag carriers of other nations until we have a flag carrier of our own. Canada simply cannot afford not to have its own merchant fleet. We condemn ourselves to mediocrity and stunted progress by failing to come to grips with this fundamental fact, not only because of our maritime tradition but because of our productive capacity and our status as a trading nation.
It stands to reason that flag carriers-leaving aside flags of convenience-like Britain, Japan, Norway, Holland, Sweden, Germany and the United States, give preference to their own products when transportation decisions have to be made. I am not arguing in favour of a chauvinistic policy or the Jones Act. I believe that a Canadian merchant marine can stand on its own feet and float on its own bottom. Tnere is money in the international transport of goods, and for an exporting and importing nation like Canada to allow its goods to be carried in foreign bottoms is to cut down on our full trading potential and to pay out excessive, and non-taxable, transport costs to boot.
What about marine insurance? We miss out and our businessmen miss out on all these counts-on carriage of our own goods, on the carriage of others' goods, on marine insurance and, as I shall mention in a minute, on shipbuilding and related services.
I have lived in a number of countries abroad and, in common with what I do at home, I invariably examine foodstuffs on the counters as I do when I am out with my wife to stock up the larder on the weekend. It has been my experience that by comparison with the products that other countries can grow and process and export, Canada's produce is just not on the shelves of the world. We see Japanese goods, United States goods, British goods, French goods, Dutch goods, but few if any Canadian consumer goods. This disturbs me. It continues to disturb me and I think we should rectify the situation. The only way to get our goods on the shelves of the world is to get them there ourselves by carrying them on our own flag carriers.
The four principles of merchandising I venture to suggest are: a quality to suit the customer, a competitive price, a regular supply and firm delivery dates. We can meet the first two objectives if we get out and see what the market wants, and this, of course, our salesmen must do; but without our own delivery vans we cannot meet the second two. We cannot guarantee regular supply and firm delivery dates by relying on trampers, for one thing, or scheduled foreign-flag merchantmen for another.
Now let us get right down to practical plans. I suggest we should start fairly modestly: the Caribbean, Central America, the east-west coast routes. Once these routes have been developed, our flag has become established and our products have dug into the market, we can venture further afield. Then what about our wheat and other grains, ore, aluminum, potassium and coal? And our paper and lumber? Just think of it. Anyone who has visited a port within the past two weeks has seen foreign-flag vessels loading these products of Canada to take them abroad. We sell these commodities in vast quantities abroad. Yet we allow others to carry these goods abroad
July 9, 1973

for us. Should we not hang our heads in shame at such a gutless display of lack of enterprise by government?
Then what about our imports, the cars, the oil, the alumina, the tropical fruits, to which we have become so accustomed? Should we not have a hand in bringing these products to our shores? I think one of our problems is that we have been a favoured nation in many ways. We have been spoiled. We have a large market next door. The carriage to that market is normally overland. But our advantages are slipping from us. This is not an assured market for all time. In addition, we risk losing our birthright unless we see just how easily we have fallen into trading patterns that are made for us by others. We are virtually a one-basket nation. Our needs and many of our surpluses flow easily north and south, most of them overland. We buy our bananas from a nation that does not even produce bananas, and most of our coffee too.
What is ailing us that we are content to live in this way at the pleasure of another instead of going at it ourselves and plowing our own furrow? We once did. We were once a proud maritime nation. We have a long and proud maritime tradition. What happened to our Bluenose generation, our lumber traders from B.C., our tea traders? We used to build ships to carry the commerce of the world. We used to build our own ships and ships for others. We are on the verge of losing that art. There were once three large yards in my area; now barely one private shipyard can be said to exist. We just have not tried hard enough.
But what really has happened? We have not had government policies that encourage investment in this type of enterprise. We have allowed ourselves to be driven off the sea. These policies must be changed. We are paying for this in terms of an international trade record that is nowhere near as striking as it should be.
I was recently shocked to hear about a contract being let for German ships to be built in Germany to carry Canadian raw material from the Arctic to Europe. And shocked is the word when we can build our own ships to carry our own goods, preferably processed goods, to the markets of the world.
To my way of thinking, a Canadian merchant marine operated privately with appropriate subsidies-and no one is going to deny that subsidies will be required in this highly competitive field today-would have a multiplier effect in terms of economic growth and the creation of employment. The merchant service itself would offer challenging careers to enterprising and venturesome Canadians. The shipbuilding industry would take root again on both our coasts, as would all the related industries. I would like to think that we would have the wit and the wisdom to use more of our primary products to make our own plate for shipbuilding, and also more for our autmo-bile industry. Why do we ship ore abroad and import it on wheels? We are letting ourselves down. There would be expanded processing in the manufacturing sector of products for export, along with the advantages which come in economies of scale. This would help with the inflation and unemployment problems which have been besetting us and which are around our necks like an albatross. Also our internal transportation industries would flourish.
Canadian Merchant Marine
Along with these developments, I can see regional development forging ahead in a manner to brighten the eyes of eastern and western maritimers and in a manner that even the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) has not dreamed about.
For a long time now we have claimed a special interest in the Caribbean. We have developed a taste for their products, but I will not mention them in the House. We use their products and they use many of ours. Here we could add a new and meaningful dimension to Canada-Caribbean relations, and in the process reduce our reliance on our neighbour immediately to the south for some of the products the Caribbean is so anxious to sell to us but which we import through the United States.
We are just not making the most of our inheritance. It is time we started to do so because in the process we will inevitably find solutions to many of the problems that beset us-the proper management of our resources, proper solutions to unemployment, to our production and trade problems. Incidentally we will find that we will also reduce inflation.
The unanimity that I have found this afternoon in the House I find most encouraging, and for these reasons I want to see this motion referred to the appropriate committee for further study and report. I hope we can arrange to do this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIVAL OF CANADIAN MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say that the minister has already discussed this question with the premiers of the Atlantic provinces, and another meeting of the officials is scheduled for later this month, in fact for July 18. The minister is interested both in moving as quickly as possible to extend opportunities for Canadian carriers and in satisfying the Atlantic premiers concerned that any change should work in their best interests.
I think it might be good to put on the record-and possibly there is no better way for one to reiterate it-the final words of Mr. Darling which he wrote on the last page of his report.
He said that the method which has been recommended for implementing a policy for Canadianization allows for varying rates of progress toward that goal. It does provide a means of escape from the static conditions created by existing legislation. However, he said, it cannot be assumed that the rapid attainment of the goal would be of unquestionable advantage in all circumstances. The purpose of the recommendation is not to provide protection for its own sake; it will be the responsibility of the industry, both management and labour, to increase efficiency and productivity, to take the lead in introducing new equipment and methods of operation that will offset the general higher level of Canadian costs.
The establishment of a deep sea merchant marine must be considered in the general context of an over-all transportation policy and, more particularly, in terms of an over-all maritime policy. Our present policy in these two regards is to utilize the world's shipping market for the transportation of goods across the seas and to support the Canadian carrier in the inland waters of Canada and the United States.

July 9, 1973
Canadian Merchant Marine
However, the government is continuously assessing the question of a Canadian merchant marine, and as recently as 1970 the Hedlin-Menzies report dealt specifically with this matter. The Hedlin-Menzies study was oriented toward the bulk trades rather than the whole range of cargo type vessels. The overriding reason for the concentration on the bulk trade was that, after initial analysis, it became evident that only very large vessels requiring a high capital investment offered prospects of their being economic. The analysis assumed that Canadian ships would operate in a competitive world shipping market and would receive revenues determined by world shipping forces. In these circumstances, the rate of return to a Canadian shipowner would be less than to a foreign owner of a similar vessel in the same trade, largely because of higher Canadian crew costs.
The report observed that while Canada has become the third largest trading nation in the world, only a small fraction of its overseas trade is being transported in Canadian registered vessels. However, at the present time our export and import trade groups are being well served by foreign flag vessels, and since our economy is so dependent upon foreign trade, the merchant shipping question must be viewed in relation to foreign trade development, and that is important. Any government policy to establish a merchant marine at very heavy expense to the Canadian taxpayer could have a disruptive economic effect by imposing the use of Canadian vessels for a substantial portion of the foreign trade.
An interdepartmental committee examined the findings of the Hedlin-Menzies report and observed that a great deal of money is being spent confirming the potential of gas, oil and ore resources in the north off-shore islands. On the assumption that it will be Canada's policy to foster the development of these resources, that export markets will be developed, and that ships will be a competitive mode to serve these export markets, there could be created a new and additional demand for shipping. This new trade would be served by specialized vessels capable of carrying various combinations of bulk cargoes and, above all, capable of sailing in Arctic waters.
The interdepartmental group concluded that, as an alternative to the present government policy towards a Canadian merchant marine, consideration should be given to, expending our experience and technical capability in the shipping and shipbuilding industries. They could be encouraged to design types of ships capable of competing, of carrying our new resources to markets, and of navigating in the arctic. It was suggested that encouragement be given to the Canadian shipping and shipbuilding community to make a start in this direction. Such a new departure might excite the enthusiasm of enterprising shipping and shipbuilding interests, and eventually create an environment in which Canadian registered ships could approach economic viability in international trading.
Subsequent to the interdepartmental review of the deep sea fleet question, the cabinet committee on government operations considered government assistance for the shipbuilding industry for the export of ships. In addition to agreeing to the extension of the export shipbuilding program, the committee agreed that an interdepartmental

task force should be established to report on the possible future role of the Canadian shipbuilding industry, including the manufacture of off-shore drill rig equipment, in terms of over-all national industrial strategy, taking into account considerations such as the international competitive environment and the degree of rationalization needed to ensure a viable and competitive industry. The task force has been led by industry, trade and commerce, with transport participating.
I am going at this point to put my comments in a different perspective. In considering the deep sea fleet question it is generally forgotten that Canada has, in fact, a substantial inland fleet.

speechtext:
I repeat that the government's maritime policies over the past years have developed the growth and technical excellence of this fleet, much on the basis of shipbuilding policies and the construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway. It now carries over 80 per cent of all trade in the international waters of Canada and the United States of America. With a view to examining further policies which would expand the opportunities for this fleet, the government commissioned the Darling Report.
The Darling Report recommended that the coasting tiade of Canada be reserved completely for Canadian flag vessels, and further that the coasting trade laws should be extended to the continental shelf and Arctic waters. These recommendations, while apparently applicable to the coasting trade, have considerable implications for the deep sea fleet issue. The Arctic waters and off-shore areas require vessels of deep sea construction, and hence if these areas were reserved for Canadian flag vessels one might assume that in any future growth of our efficient inland fleet there could be foreseen a potential of a deep sea fleet. Again, however, this matter must be considered along with our resource policies.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), in a speech before the Dominion Marine Association and the U.S. Lake Carriers Association in January, 1973, expressed the view that important resource developments are in the offing which will present very great opportunities for the Canadian maritime industry, and there is a general consensus that the substantial part of this work should be performed by Canadians.
However, he said, the benefits to be gained from new policies to reserve these new and expanding frontiers to Canadian vessels could only be realized if the maritime industry responds with new technology and suitable ships

to move these resources. In the studies concerning the economic and technical requirements of these specialized ships, close contact is being maintained between the government and private industry.
The government is actively interested in developing new maritime policies where these can be shown to have over-all benefits for Canada. But in policy examination and in subsequent action we must rely, in the final analysis, on the co-operation and initiative of the Canadian maritime industry.
Having said all these things, Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to go further into the details of the 1970 Hedlin-Men-zies Report. It concluded that the Canadian net benefits generated by Canadian merchant vessels are extremely sensitive to cost projections, and Canadian rates of return can be significantly reduced-[DOT]

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: EXPORT LICENSING OF CERTAIN AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I extend to the members of the House my appreciation. We have now reverted to motions and I should like to make a short statement regarding further export control of certain agricultural commodities.
As I indicated to the House on Friday, we are taking stock on an urgent basis of our own inventory of protein supplies, including the additional commodities placed under export control by the United States last Thursday. I refer to the United States announcement that 41 categories of commodities, including edible oils, animal fats and livestock protein feeds, would be subject to export control effective July 5. We are now able to make a better assessment of supplies and requirements as a result of requests for permits which have been received.
In view of the decision of the United States to extend their control, the government has decided to take further precautionary measures and to place certain additional items, including some edible oils, animal fats and livestock protein feeds, on an export licensing basis for the present time. A list of the additional items which are subject to export control from midnight, July 9, is being tabled with this statement.
With respect to these new items under control, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will consider export permit applications for these commodities provided that applications are supported by copies of contracts in existence on June 29 for shipments up to October
15.	As in the case of commodities placed under control Friday, June 29, exporters are requested to forward applications for export permits, supported by copies of contracts in existence on June 29, to the export and import permits division of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
Shipments of goods which are being placed under control today and are in the process of being loaded for export, or are in transit to an export port, will be permitted to go forward provided satisfactory evidence is given that contracts were in existence prior to June 29.
Applications for permits covering other contracts will be examined on a case by case basis. It continues to be the government's intention to ensure adequate supplies to meet Canadian requirements and to take into account the needs of Canada's traditional foreign customers.
Regarding the commodities placed under export control on June 29, we will issue export permits for rapeseed and flaxseed provided these applications are supported by copies of contracts in existence on June 29 for shipments up to October 15. We are continuing to monitor the situation closely and may find it necessary at a later stage to reduce the quantities allowed for export of these commodities should it be essential in order to ensure adequate supplies to meet Canadian requirements.
5432

July 9, 1973
Exports
Due to the shortage of soya beans and soya bean meal and the situation arising in Canada following the decision of the United States to limit exports, we will not be in a position to issue export permits for these products.
We are completing the assessment of the availability and requirements for rapeseed and linseed cake and meal and fishmeal, taking into account the requests for export permits which are being received, and a further announcement will be forthcoming.
I should like to stress that these actions by Canada are necessary precautionary measures to safeguard our market against distortions in world trade in protein feeds that may arise as a result of the shortages of animal protein feeds and United States control measures. The export controls are designed as temporary actions pending the stabilizing of the situation and the arrival of new crop supplies on the Canadian market.

subtopic: EXPORT LICENSING OF CERTAIN AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's announcement tonight was, I suppose, inevitable. It was like the night following day.
In response to the action taken by the United States there seems, once again, to be little the Canadian government is in a position to do except to react. We have become too dependent on that country in respect to many edible oils and high protein foods. Now that their domestic supplies are threatened, and export controls imposed, we must protect our inadequate supplies until the situation has been rationalized. Some farmers have complained that feed costs are rising so fast that unless some relief is afforded them they will face bankruptcy. The rise in costs these last few months has been astronomical, of a magnitude unprecedented in decades.
Producers, on the other hand, are enjoying high prices for a change, a rare experience for some of them. If controls limit their prices unduly, they will not be encouraged to increase production, but this in the long run is the only solution. The only way that the situation can be rationalized in the long run is to increase production of these high protein crops and feeds. Unlike costs in the monopolistic and oligopolistic sector of our economy, the commodities that we are talking about tonight are those that operate in a market where the price is determined by supply and demand.
In these cases, the only way of meeting the demand at home and increasing our proportion of total world market supply is to increase production very substantially in this country. The situation in which we find ourselves tonight is really that of the government's chickens coming home to roost. This government did everything it possibly could to discourage oilseed processing plants in Canada.

subtopic: EXPORT LICENSING OF CERTAIN AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPORT LICENSING OF CERTAIN AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
It did everything it could to discourage the kind of diversification and increased potential that this country needs and which would be good for Canadian farmers, both at the present time and in the years to come. What is required now is obviously greater imagination and initiative on the part of the government, policies designed to assist through technology the development of strains of

soybean, for example, which are resistant to cold and can be grown in our great western provinces as well as in southwestern Ontario.
We hope the government will learn something from this crisis in which we find ourselves. We hope it will not drift along and wait for the next act of the United States to which it will react. We hope this time it will show some imagination and divert some of the money which is being used in less productive ways to agricultural programs to assist Canadian farmers to expand and diversify their products, which would be very useful to them and rewarding in every respect in the years to come.
While we reluctantly accept this announcement, and without commenting on the retroactive feature of it, we hope the government will take to heart the lesson we have learned, stop this policy of drift from crisis to crisis, start showing some initiative and imagination, and give the Canadian farmers the kind of support they really deserve.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the announcement tonight by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) highlights the incompetence of this government and its mismanagement and bad direction of the farm economy. The minister is in the unfortunate position of having to develop a policy which in essence tries to cover the mistakes and correct the inadequacies of the minister in charge of the wheat board. If this House should do anything tonight, it should call for the resignation of that minister.

speechtext:
I hear catcalls from my right, from the people who refused to put rye and the oilseeds under the Canadian Wheat Board, and refused any move toward orderly marketing to ensure a price for the farmer which would encourage him to produce those products which Canadians need.
We are the victims of a nineteenth century approach to our agricultural economy. We are the victims of planning for scarcity, which is what the government has planned for in the past number of years. They told the farmers not to produce wheat. They also told them not to produce rapeseed or barley. This is on the record. They now come with their export permits, their lack of capacity and ability to provide Canadians with the protein that is needed for our livestock industry. We fought for a decent freight rate policy for western Canada to move our processed oil and protein meal to eastern Canada. We had to fight on our own. If as a result of the situation we face tonight there is a redirection of policy for farmers and agriculture, that will be our only gain.
I have no confidence in the minister and his export permits. While the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is pleading for the tolerance of this House so that he may issue export permits for vital farm products, the minister in charge of the wheat board is planning programs and policies that will destroy the control and administration of the Canadian Wheat Board over the

handling of feed grains. At the same time as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is asking western farmers to accept his controls, the minister in charge of the wheat board is preparing to destroy the very essence of orderly marketing upon which the western farmer depends.
I await the announcements of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. However, if they are of the kind indicated by press releases up to this time, I will not have any further confidence in the minister in charge of the wheat board or the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who really does not know what he is talking about.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that the government allows problems to worsen in the extreme before it reacts. For the past few months in this House, every week, if not every day, the serious problem of rising food production costs has been emphasized. Many questions have been put to the various ministers responsible, but we have always received unsatisfactory answers that gave no hint of a solution to this serious problem.
Now we are suffering from the consequences of this practice of leaving problems unsolved. Not only are the farmers in a difficult situation, with production costs rising and the cost-price squeeze getting tighter, but the consumers are also being hit by this rise in production costs, and from all sides we hear the farmers making representations and stating that, in despair, they will abandon their farms unless a solution is found quickly.
Mr. Speaker, I met yesterday with a group of producers from my constituency who told me of their fears over this problem. The cost of protein feeds is now very high, thus contributing to the unprecedented price rise for products of all kinds.
This evening, the minister has announced that in view of the American government's imposition of permits on the export of certain high-protein products, Canada is also forced to impose restrictions, until the results of the coming harvest are known, by obliging exporters to apply for permits to respect contracts signed before June 29.
So, I say this: to my mind, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) should have been advised much earlier of the situation; he should have taken steps to force those exporters to keep a huge quantity of those protein-rich products and so enable Canada to keep up its impetus towards increased food production, and agricultural production in every sphere.
A while ago, I heard the former speaker talk about the serious problems of western producers; but the problem also exists in the eastern provinces. That is why I say the problem is very serious and I urge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to study it further and more intensively with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) with a view to taking other steps, as soon as possible, and ensuring Canada an adequate production to enable all producers to meet their obligations, to meet the needs in food products of the people, and also make reasonable profits, that an end might be put to that painful and

Mr. Speaker, I therefore approve what steps have just been taken. Moreover, I hope, in fact, I am convinced that the government will get the support of this House in taking whatever measures are deemed conducive to remedy the situation, measures that will not be band-aids on a wooden leg.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I say I hope the minister who made a statement on motions a few minutes ago will recognize the spirit of co-operation shown on this side of the House. We welcome statements on motions, and today is no exception.
It is somewhat coincidental that I should rise tonight to talk about redistribution so soon after we have heard a statement on motions, and various comments by hon. members in response, on a subject which has to do with agriculture. It seems to me that if our relations with the United States were on a better footing it would have been unnecessary for the minister to have made this statement. Our neighbours to the south seem to be much more progressive in their attitude toward agriculture than we are.
One of the most fundamental problems facing our nation today is the fact that the most productive parts of the country are so sparsely represented in the House of Commons. I could easily make tonight what might be considered a parochial speech, a speech which might delight some members of the House though it might not appeal to the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), on the effect of the bill before us as it pertains to the constituency of Gander-Twillingate. But I believe we are talking about a subject which is fundamental to confederation, one which is causing frustration to Canadians and members of parliament today and having to do with the balance of representation in this chamber.
I take fairly strong issue with some of the speeches which have been made here in recent days. They have been, perhaps, a bit small minded, may be a bit political for the sake of some immediate political gain. I suggest we recognize the fact that parts of Canada which are extremely productive, which still have a tremendous capacity to produce, do not enjoy the representation they deserve. Looking to my right, I see an hon. member who has already taken part in this debate, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling); the "Darling of rural

Canada", we might call him in our caucus, and perhaps this makes it unnecessary for any other member from rural Canada to come forward with a presentation.
However, there is a bill before us dealing with redistribution and I wish to present a few arguments to induce members to look at the representation in the House in a somewhat different light. If the bill were not passed, then in accordance with the process now in being the representation accorded to various areas of the country would be reduced. I am giving only one example when I mention my own province, where there would be a reduction from seven seats to six, though the population has almost doubled since Newfoundland became part of Canada in 1949.
But that fact is irrelevant to my argument that a seat should be lost in Newfoundland, or Manitoba or Saskatchewan. I am suggesting that if a federal system is to continue to operate in this country it will be necessary to take a serious look at the balance of representation in the House of Commons. Unless this is done, a challenge will be presented to the basis of confederation. Unless those areas which constitute productive parts of the country, areas which possess resource capacity, are given a proportionately fairer share of representation, I consider we are not heading in the right direction.
There are many reasons for saying that the issues facing us in the Atlantic region, for example, are not receiving due attention because our members do not carry sufficient political weight in terms of numbers. You can talk all you like about agriculture, for example, but if there are only 20 or 30 members representing truly agricultural constituencies it is almost impossible to influence government policy effectively.
You can rest relatively assured that these questions will not occupy the main attention of the government, mainly because of the fact that it makes little difference whether the government stands for agriculture or is against agriculture. It recognizes it can get elected without the agricultural vote. On the Atlantic coast we have 32 seats out of a grand total of 264; we have 12 per cent of the representatives in the Canadian House of Commons. It makes little difference to the federal government, whether it be this government or some other government, in which direction the Atlantic vote is steered in approving or disapproving federal policies. As long as this is the case you can rest assured that the Atlantic provinces or the western provinces are going to be mere appendices to the federal system.
I want to tell Your Honour and the House of Commons that unless there is some major departure from either the philosophy or the attitude of governments as they have existed in the past or as they exist today, or some major departure from the present system of representation in the House of Commons, then the alienation that is felt in Quebec, in the Atlantic provinces and in the western provinces will not only continue but will continue to grow. This is what concerns me more than the bill before us here today.
I am very sorry that my colleague who is a member of my own party is not in the House today, and if he were in the House I have a feeling that the least I would do would

be to strip him of some of the medals that he has gained from some of his political wars. I have read with care the remarks of my hon. colleague about the very narrow minded attitude that was expressed, and I am worried not only about that attitude, but I am afraid it might become the attitude taken by some other members of this House of Commons.
Anybody who suggests that the representation in the Canadian House of Commons should be based totally, primarily and solely on population really does not deserve to enjoy the benefits of a federal system and be part of Canada. This particular problem is so much more complex and so much more complicated than that. If you read the acts and regulations governing the terms of reference of the people who tried to recommend redistribution, you will see nowhere any guidelines governing the approach of these people in recommending redistribution.
My colleague the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), in the meetings we have had, I do not mind saying quite openly has always made the point that population should not be the only consideration for redistribution of Canadian seats or representation in the House of Commons.
As I say, the whole process of redistribution is so much more complex. What I would like to see growing out of this debate and the committee report are some guidelines for a future body, whether it be a committee of the House of Commons or the redistribution agency that is given legislative power by the House of Commons, as to what should be the appropriate considerations for representation in the House of Commons.
I agree with my colleague from Peel South (Mr. Blen-karn) that population has always to be a dominating factor in determining representation in the House of Commons. I think it is grossly unfair for my colleague to have
200,000	people in his district and for me to be representing only 75,000 people. All other factors being equal, I think this is grossly unfair. Nevertheless, I know there are members from the urban parts of Canada, from Edmonton, Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal and Hamilton, who are representing people in excess of the 75,000 average we from the Atlantic provinces represent.
There are other factors as well. For anybody to suggest that Prince Edward Island should lose any of its representation I think would be rejecting the whole process of Canadian history. Prince Edward Island is a province that elected to come into confederation at the beginning, at a time when we as a province were waiting to see-and this could be a quotation in all the history books-if we could get the best deal possible out of confederation. We did not have the gumption to become part of Canada until 1949, but we are now proud to be part of Canada. Certainly you cannot argue that this historic fact is not one to be considered when you are determining representation in the House of Commons. I think this goes for those western provinces as well that elected to become part of this great country, in some cases almost a century ago.
I represent a district that is one of the largest districts in the House of Commons; at least, I get $800 extra on my expense allowance every year on this account. I think I am one of 22 other districts whose members get extra allowances based on the fact that they have such a heavy
July 9, 1973

geographic responsibility. I have oiten wondered if the hon. member from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), which by the way is one of the great resource frontiers of North America and the western world, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), my friend from the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), my friend from Churchill (Mr. Taylor), and other members who represent these districts, have great difficulty in giving their constituents any representation and service under our federal system.
As a matter of fact, any time our friends from urban centres would like to visit my riding or any riding similar to mine and spend a week experiencing the difficulty of travelling around a district with the geography of any of the Atlantic provinces, or of most of the western provinces for that matter, they are quite welcome to do so. I would like to suggest that this would change their philosophy about more representation in urban Canada based on the need for service.
It is almost impossible for members from the rural parts of this country to give anything like an adequate service to their constituents. My colleague from St. John's West (Mr. Carter) is sitting here right now. People from the urban parts of his riding, unlike the rural parts, can walk into the Unemployment Insurance Office, a post office, a hospital, or any of the facilities of either the provincial or the federal government, with no transportation difficulty at all because all are within easy access.
I represent a riding that requires me to travel about
7,000	or 10,000 miles in a period of about two months. During that time I might get into each community for 10 or 15 minutes. I represent a total of nine island communities, and one of these communities is in the most easterly part of Canada, Fogo Island, 12 miles out in the Atlantic Ocean. On that island alone there are 12 little communities. It is a day's work to go to the island; it is three days' work to travel around the island. There are all the disadvantages of poor roads, the communications difficulties of a remote community. After a couple of days there I might get into each community for five or 10 minutes; then I have to go on to another community. Then I have a day's work to get back. After spending that much effort I have serviced about 5,000 people.
The basic reason we have to go into our rural communities is that the people expect to see you, though you certainly cannot give them anything like the commendable service you can give people in urban communities. You can walk around the average riding in Ottawa in a week, almost going from door to door. You can knock on every door and ask every old lady or every young woman or every eligible voter what their problems are. You can get on the open line program the next morning and talk about practically any subject.
However, Labrador is about as big as the Atlantic provinces put together. Even if you had the energies of Frobisher and the dedication of Dr. Grenville, it would take you the whole summer to get into each community for five minutes. This is the kind of situation we face, yet we have people like my colleague and others getting up in the House of Commons and talking about population being the only basis for redistribution of seats.
