Although I have been talking about history, population and geography, we also have resources in our area. My colleague and others have stood up and said you cannot consider the fact that you represent resources. You do not represent oil wells, you do not represent wheat fields, you do not represent mines and you do not represent timber resources, any more than you represent pavement or airports. I would like to say to this House and to the Canadian people that that is exactly what we do represent.
If we are not willing to represent the resources of our country, why do we not recognize that some other countries might be interested in these resources? We talk about foreign ownership. We have a population in Labrador the size of a small city, 25,000 to 30,000 people. Labrador feeds most of the mineral wealth of great cities. Most of the resources in the city of Pittsburgh come from Labrador. Most of the water requirements of the northeast coast of North America come from Labrador.
A couple of years ago we started and almost completed a billion-dollar project. In 1972 the Churchill Falls project, which was the largest project in the world outside of the American space program, employed 6,600 men and women on site in Churchill Falls. That project is going to be completed by 1976 or 1977 and will supply the electrical needs of the whole of the northeast coast of North America.
This project has never been discussed in the House of Commons. The matter has been mentioned by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador and on a few other occasions by other colleagues of mine, although they have barely mentioned it. No one has mentioned what the dividends are to the Canadian people, how the ownership is constituted or what the United States involvement is. We have "half a member" in this House of Commons to talk about a project which is worth $1 billion.
The Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory are the great frontiers of North America, with all the mineral, oil and other wealth we need for the next 100 years. Yet we have only two members in this House of Commons representing these two territories which are larger than the rest of Canada. Do hon. members mean to tell me that this is not an issue when we talk about redistribution and representation?
How many people sitting around the cabinet table have an input in respect to the Northwest Territories, the Yukon Territory, or Labrador, the great resource frontiers? I say these factors are much more important in the long run to Canada than the proposition of the population we represent. I think if someone gave us a chance to represent some of the cities of Canada, three or four of us could make a pretty good job of it.
In talking about government representation, may I say I represent an area of Canada-and I think I speak for most of my colleagues from rural areas-which is practically without any form of government other than provincial and municipal. A federal and provincial system of government is almost unnecessary. In parts of Canada today municipal governments are highly sophisticated and have the ability to carry on the system almost without the

Almost every day in my office I receive 40 or 50 letters about every kind of problem one might imagine-social, welfare, unemployment and every other type. If someone wants to build a home on a piece of land next door, or if a lady has a problem with a neighbour, she writes to me rather than take it up with the welfare office or the municipal office. She writes to her member of parliament.
I am perhaps dramatizing the situation to show the problems that the rural representative on the federal side has in the House of Commons, but there is hardly a problem one could mention with which we are not confronted. I had a phone call from a constituent today who asked me about buying land from his next door neighbour. He wanted to find out who owned it, how much it cost and how he would go about buying it. All that urban members hear about are abortion matters, urban problems, housing and so on. We have these problems too, but we have to deal with real people and many other problems. Perhaps there was a television program which did not go over too well in our area. We might receive 100 letters from people telling us they did not like it, that they could not make up their mind about it, or something like that. As I say, we are dealing with real people and real problems.
Perhaps the only contact they have with the government is through their federal member, or in some cases their provincial member. I am not an unusual member of parliament. One could visit the office of any member of parliament from rural Canada and find that their phones are constantly ringing. They have two secretaries who are run ragged. Other offices are busy but they do not have the same type of problems we have. I am sure that in the city of Ottawa today the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) does not have to deal with these basic "gut" problems that we have in our areas.

I know he does not deal with the major problems, but I do not think he deals with the minor ones either. My colleague from Vancouver South told me-as a matter of fact I remember it quite vividly-of his concern that the redistribution which took place did not consider the concept of the community. He told me he felt it was necessary to do more than say to somebody that you are going to redistribute seats in the House of Commons and have 70,000 or 90,000 people in a riding, or 80,000 people with latitude above and beyond that median, because there is something called community in Canada.
The community of St. John's has 100,000 people. It is a beautiful, neat district. If the way we redistribute seats is to give 80,000 people in the city of St. John's to one member, another 20,000 people at the other end are cut away even though these people all have common values and common economic, political and social problems. These 20,000 other people are stuck into another district and have nothing in common with the people there. If that is how we distribute seats in Canada, I suggest there must be a major overhaul in respect to Canadian representation.
I do not wish to harp on this point, but I do want to say that in the overall distribution of seats the values of the Canadian people must be considered. From listening to the

arguments which have been presented during this debate one might draw the conclusion that everyone should live in the cities of Canada.

You know exactly who I am talking about. I will not repeat the names of my colleagues because we have had enough of this. Everyone knows that some people feel very strongly that population is the only factor in redistribution. But I contend we must look at the values of the Canadian people too. Many people want to live in the rural parts of Canada. I predict that within the next decade many people who are now living in the urban parts of the country will want to seek the solace, benefit and beauty of rural Canada. My colleague from Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) talked about the quality of life, and I am sure there is no one more qualified to talk about it than he.
In conclusion, I wish to spend about five or ten minutes in trying to establish what are some of the factors I feel must be considered. I suggest to my colleague the House leader that I do not think the bill goes far enough. I shall not be satisfied until we have taken this thing through to the point where we have discussed all the factors influencing redistribution. I shall not be satisfied with legislation limited to the year 1974. I shall not be satisfied until we have legislative power given some direction by the Canadian House of Commons.
I have tried to touch on history, population, geography, resources, other governments' involvement in certain areas, the vagaries of the Canadian people and community of interest in certain areas. These are factors that I believe should govern the redistribution of seats. In conclusion, I want to touch, partly parochially, on two particular problems that strike home to me very forcefully.
One is resources, and all of the implications of resources as a factor in the Canadian governmental system. We became part of Canada-if I sort of edge my way into the ranks of Nova Scotians, Prince Edward Islanders and New Brunswickers-back in 1867 and thereafter. Newfoundland, as a province, did not become part of Canada until 1949, and ever since that date we have suffered the most chronic unemployment situation in the western world.
Today we have the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and statisticians talking about the fact that there is full employment in some parts of Canada. They are even talking about labour shortages. At the same time in the Atlantic provinces-and here I am sort of generalizing a bit-we have about 10 per cent unemployment. The situation gets worse in the winter months and better in the summer months. The best we can say is that we have a very heavy seasonal unemployment problem, which most of us can just tolerate because of the welfare scheme of the Canadian nation. But we do not like it because our people want to work.
There has never been a government since 1867 that had the gumption to take issue with the real problems facing this country, particularly the problems facing our part of the country. This has to do with the fact that we are part of the federal system, in which tariffs are designed to satisfy the needs of the heavily industrialized parts of the
July 9, 1973

country. I stress that we have nothing in the world against this. We are also part of this country where the economic policies of the government are designed to satisfy the majority of the people. We have nothing in the world against that. We want the people in Toronto and Montreal to be at work. We want the people in central Canada to be at work. We are part of this system in which the monetary policies of the government have to be designed to satisfy the great majority of the Canadian people, and we have nothing in the world against that either.
From time to time new monetary policies are designed to cool off inflation, to increase interest rates, and to make money tight. But what happens to us is that, each time there is a moderate fluctuation in monetary policy or tariff policy, we are getting it right in the rear end. And the same thing happens in western Canada. We end up bearing the burden of Canadian economic policies. I repeat that nobody since 1867 has ever had the gumption to come out and say there were going to vary their policies to satisfy new needs, or to satisfy our local needs.
I am predicting that even with the efforts of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion the problem of unemployment will continue to exist long after I have sat down in my seat tonight. Again I say that nobody has had the gumption to remedy this situation, the reason being that it is not politically necessary to draw up these kinds of policies to satisfy those parts of Canada whose people have problems. Some ten years from now I will be back fishing, or teaching school, or doing something else, and we will still have the same problems in the Atlantic provinces simply because it is not politically necessary for the central government to cater to the Atlantic provinces.
The city of Toronto has more parliamentary seats than Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island combined. The two Canadian cities of Toronto and Montreal have more parliamentary seats than all four Atlantic provinces. Why would it be necessary for the government to sit around a table and worry about economic policies as they affect the Atlantic provinces?
We acknowledge the fact that our colleagues from down east, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), are doing their best. I have absolute respect for them. They are men who put a great deal of energy into our Canadian system. But the fact of the matter is they do not have the capacity, the ability, the energy, or the time to represent the Atlantic provinces in a way that will bring about any substantial change in the direction taken by our provinces.
I have mentioned Labrador. It has huge deposits of iron ore and great mineral wealth that few hon. members even know about. You think we are a poor province? You can bet your boots we are not a poor province. The only member in this House outside the Atlantic region who has ever dealt with our resources in a knowledgeable manner is the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), who usually thinks about a quarter of a century ahead.
We have this great resource in Labrador which is being harvested in the raw form, and shipped down to Pittsburgh in ships and trains. Nobody in our province is getting any real value from it. Would this situation contin-

We have the continental shelf resources on the east coast. We have the resources under our sea bed that are now in dispute between the provincial governments and the federal government. How often do we hear members talking about them in the House of Commons? Not only do they not talk about them, but it is almost out of order when you stand up in your place in this House and talk about marine resources. Fish is almost a dirty four-letter word, like the "fuddle-duddle" that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came out with. You simply do not talk about fish because that concerns the poorer element of the Atlantic coast.
We do not have 50 or 60 members standing up in their places and embarrassing Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the Prime Minister with the power of persuasion, and with their convictions about Atlantic resources. We do not have the muscle, the horsepower. How often have you heard the Prime Minister talk about marine resources? He does not know what the continental shelf is. He does not understand one bit about fish. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) would not dirty his hands with fish and continental shelf resources. As a matter of fact, very few people in central Canada ever bother about them. Mr. Speaker, if I ever make the Globe and Mail on fish I will stand up on a question of privilege and say that something has gone wrong. Watergate, Viet Nam, and Mr. Pearson's involvement are big issues; fish is not a big issue.
Some of my colleagues and I have just returned from Iceland. Some of my venturesome colleagues have a little blood in them. They are descendants of people who came across to Newfoundland and really started the development of this great continent of North America. We asked the CBC if they would like to send a cameraman with us. Although we were not interested in political advantage, they said they could not send anybody.
The day after I came back I had a little time and I looked up CBC programming and found they were going to devote 12 hours to programs on the Moslem religion. I suppose that must cost about $4 million or $5 million. Yet they could not afford to send anybody with us. It would have cost them $3,000 to send a camera crew to Iceland where we wanted to compare the problems of the Icelandic fishery with our problems on the east coast of Canada. It all boils down to the question of political power and muscle. We just do not have any. If anybody is interested in redistributing seats, I think they should start looking at the country from a different perspective. I know that I am talking language that western Canadians also understand.
I am going to complete my remarks with a little comment about something called urban drift. All over the world for the last half century we have had what has been called the urban drift. Most people have a kind of Arctic lemming tendency, but people have to go to the big centres. Some people go there because they must; they are unemployed at home. A lot of our people from Newfoundland have gone to Toronto. Traditionally there has been a great exodus of east coast Canadians to Toronto. But in the last few years, whether hon. members have recognized

July 9, 1973
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension it or not there has been a tendency for people to start to look in our direction.
It always amazes me that the guys who grow their hair a bit longer, the guys we call hippies, were the first people who started to question some aspects of our material trip, our urban trip. On the east coast of Canada-I do not know what people experience on the west coast-we began to find that the hippies went out to little island communities that had been vacated by our people as a result of resettlement and other programs that the government had drawn up which encouraged people to move away frcm rural communities. Small farmers were discouraged from living on their farms and there was general discouragement from living in rural Canada. The government encouraged people to move away from rural communities, and we found that the progressive types were those who moved in.
I wonder if anyone here has read any of Mr. Thoreau's works? I am referring to his leaving society in the 1840's- Walden was the name of the place-and going to live as the hippie of his day in uninhabited parts, in the almost uncivilized wilderness of this country. The hippies have started to go back to the rural parts of this country where they have found something of value. They did not find smokestacks, congestion, traffic jams, heat waves, and all this kind of nonsense. They found pleasant people, uninhabited countryside, homes and places where they could till the soil and lead a normal, traditional life. They found a quality of life which our ancestors came here to seek. Many people in the mad drift for urbanism forgot all about this. I am saying that there is a tendency, one the government should recognize, for people to want to get away from some aspects of urban living.
I heard today my colleague from the south coast of Newfoundland, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), telling some of us at a little private gathering that he had spoken with the leader of the Russian people who said that even in that country they had tried to put some kind of a brake on the growth of urbanism but have not succeeded very well because some of the forces that encourage urbanization are almost uncontrollable.
In all countries of the world there has been a tendency to try to control the drift toward urbanization. Today we are experiencing two forces. First, there is the attempt by people to try to control urbanism because provincial or municipal governments do not seem to be able to control it. They do not know what to do with it. It is getting to the point where we just cannot control problems which tend to become magnified in the large urban centres.
I am saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the government of this country or any future government wanted to lend a small measure of support to the encouragement of rural living, they should start showing their real concern by placing more emphasis on the rural voter. This is what I wish to say in conclusion. I think it would be worthwhile, instead of supporting the philosophy which has been expounded here by some hon. members that we should base ourselves on the principle of representation by population, to consider trying to move in the opposite direction,

because year after year governments have shown a tendency to allow urban growth and drift of population towards urban centres.
Perhaps we should say to the Atlantic and to the western provinces that we will not reduce their representation, that we will increase it and give the urban member more support staff to carry on his role. If we were to do that, then I would say that there would be much more policy and economic, social and political direction emanating from the government which would be in tune with the country and in tune with the views of the majority of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that there was an obvious need to delay the application of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act.
In fact, several of my colleagues in this House have stressed various points, and have argued, in my opinion, in a most reasonable manner. They have spoken of demographic factors, they have distinguished between the rural and urban regions, and I believe Mr. Speaker, that all the hon. member were right.
Indeed, it is most difficult to give the usual consideration to the possibility of changing electoral boundaries when one considers the extraordinary size of our country and all the other human factors.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, before implementing the recommendations of the commission it is absolutely essential that the present legislation be completely revised, since an extremely important factor-and I would like to stress this-is forgotten, namely the different racial origins in of the people of this country. Mr. Speaker, by virtue of the underlying principles of the legislation, it could happen, in theory, that the French-Canadian element of the country, for example, would have almost no representation in this House.
That is a major factor, an extremely important factor, for if the principle were applied right now in the province of Quebec, for example, there would be two fewer constituencies, and if circumstances dictated that the population of Quebec were more stagnant than that of Ontario or the other provinces, it could happen that the number of members from Quebec in this House would drop alarmingly, and we would thus be admitting that those who no longer believe in Canada are completely right. There is, therefore, an urgent need to thoroughly revise this Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, so as to take basic factors into consideration. The hon. member who preceded me spoke in particular of the problems of Newfoundland; it is true that this province has special problems. The same may be true for other provinces.
I would specially like to stress the case of Quebec, for, in my opinion, it is extremely important to maintain the ethnic entities which are the very basis of our country.
Therefore, electoral boundaries should be based on that and the various basic elements in this country should be given the guaranty that they will be represented in this Parliament.
The population cannot be the essential factor to be considered and I believe the mistake in the present legisla-

tion consists in giving this factor too much importance, for on that account, Mr. Speaker, if one always relied on such a factor and gave it such importance, how could one consider all international organizations?
How for instance could the United Nations be an entity where each country is given distinct and full representation, if the population factors were considered? In that case, only extremely populous countries would have all rights.
Therefore, in this country of ours, made up of the provinces, we should consider those entities with respect to the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, so that each part or each area in this country is sure of having adequate representation in this House.

And it would be flying in the face of facts to refuse to make a distinction between rural and urban areas. I wonder to what extent the commission takes that factor in consideration. I think that the commission must divide by x a population of 22 million inhabitants, but the sociological and economic factors which must absolutely be considered when a redistribution is involved seem to be completely neglected by the commissioners. I think that a lot of representations were made in this House recently with respect to business already in progress to have the House consider certain factors which we think are very important.
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension
The government responded with this bill presently before us to postpone the changes for 18 months. But to what extent during those 18 months will the commission be invited to consider the views expressed in this House?
And I think that it would be inadequate and even also ridiculous to have a postponement of 18 months if no changes are brought about in the methods used by the commissioners to determine electoral boundaries.
I think it is very important during those 18 months that the government ensure that methods used are well monitored so that the commission will recognize that it is impossible to have the same number of voters in both rural and urban ridings, considering all the differences, all the problems involved. But as a Quebecer I must ask that the representation of 74 seats be not reduced in the process, considering the original proposals made by the commission. I think it is important that every member make that recommendation and urge the government to consider the importance of representation first. If we assess the number of our voters we realize that most members represent very large ridings and that reducing the number of seats is out of the question. To the contrary, we would be inclined to think that it would be wiser and more logical to see that the number of members be increased, which would be fairer and more efficient.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make on this bill, and I hope it will not merely be a deferment to allow the commission to act as it pleases, as it does at present. I hope the government will see to it that when readjusting the electoral boundaries of a given area the commission will consider the economic and social factors and as far as possible arrange in groups people whose mentalities are identified by themselves.
At present, the commission has ignored all these factors and we are wondering how responsible people can contemplate such a redistribution. If you have a little respect for the people, you must certainly separate them as it is done now, exactly like animals. In my view, we must consider these factors, reorganize our areas in order to have them better represented and so that they get from the government much more concrete results and also in order that members, from whatever party, may better fulfill their duties and responsibilities. I do not doubt that each member wishes to represent efficiently the people who have elected him, but starting with a logical electoral map, it will be possible to give a logical representation.

To that I say a very hearty "amen." I feel so strongly that we need to improve the redistribution process that I want to give my support to the bill even though it means delaying redistribution.
As a result of the report of the Electoral Boundaries Commission, as has been so eloquently and interestingly enunciated by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) tonight, we are now facing a very serious situation in modern Canada, namely the deruralization of Canada. I will explain what I mean by that. I speak as an urban member from Alberta. Alberta after redistribution holds the same total of 19 seats, but the city ridings of Calgary and Edmonton gain three seats at the expense of the rural ridings. In other words, rural Alberta will have three less seats. One might think that as an urban member I would be in favour of this since we would have higher representation from the kind of area I represent. Nothing could be further from the truth.
I want to indicate tonight the kind of objection I raised on April 2 when I made a personal submission before the Electoral Boundaries Commission of Alberta. I will speak about that at the conclusion of my remarks. The thrust of my argument is why I am in favour of this bill and why I am in favour of helping rural Canada to regain the strength it has been losing.
The rural constituencies are redrawn in a map we have before us. They are too large geographically, with the result they will be impossible to service. The disproportionately large populations in the rural constituencies compared with the smaller populations in the urban constituencies does a disservice to the needs of rural Alberta. This situation prevails across the country.
An assumption was made by the drafters that the urban population will grow. This also is a disservice to the rural constituencies. It is not the function of the commission to make this assumption. Indeed, I think the quality of life in Canada is hurt by setting up structures that make it more difficult for rural areas to maintain their viability. I argue the reverse, namely that it is in the interests of a balanced spectrum of life in Canada to protect the rural areas against the forces of an urbanized, technological society which is now prevailing against them. It is not the least of the functions of a rural member of parliament to protect the interests of rural constituents and legislate on their behalf.
It was said in this debate the other day that if the present redistribution were to be carried out, we would have in this House in a few years time 90 per cent of representation from 12 major cities in Canada. Everybody knows of the drift to urban centres. This would be the

consequence of a strict following of representation by population. Not the least of the consequences of that unfortunate situation would be that we would hear less in this House of the famous commodities of wheat and fish. As important as those two commodities is the transportation and marketing so necessary to ensure the economic strength of Canada across the board.
There is not only economic concern here but the very quality of life itself. The social problems of our cities have been mushrooming as a result of a very rapid expansion which is all to well known. I make an earnest plea that in passing this bill we encourage the government to set up the kind of commission that would be responsive to the total needs of Canada and would go beyond the very narrow limitation of thinking that is embraced by this slogan, "rep by pop".
As a western Canadian, it would be easy to second the observation made by Dr. Norman Ward, professor of political science at the University of Saskatchewan and vicechairman of the Saskatchewan Electoral Boundaries Commission, a very astute man. He said:
It is clear, in sum, that the western provinces, compared with the others, have not had their fair share of parliamentary representation in either the Commons or the Senate.
I want to support that argument. Much as I agree with the thrust of Professor Ward's observation that western representation needs to be increased, we must consider the over-all good of the country rather than this preoccupation with making the House of Commons totally representative of accelerating urbanization in this country.
I do not want to turn my back on the urban members of this House, of which I am one. Obviously our people need better service. We are servicing a great many people. But one of the ways in which we could move ahead in this area would be for the Electoral Boundaries Commission to apply the tolerance level more generously than they did, certainly in Alberta. In Alberta they tried to make constituencies with a population of roughly 85,000. It was much too even between the urban and rural constituencies. We argued they should have gone 25 per cent above in the population of urban constituencies and 25 per cent below in the case of rural, but they did not do that. That is one of the reasons so many members from Alberta, myself included, are adamantly opposed to the kind of redistribution we were offered.
The hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) made a very strong case which was the subject of some criticism. It is a very hard job to try and service increasingly populous urban areas. In this interim process we can come up with something better. Why does the government delay in providing constituency offices and help for members of parliament who are now acting as ombudsmen as well as parliamentarians and communicators with their constituencies? We are facing all the problems the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) so interestingly illuminated tonight. We need more help in the urban constituencies particularly. If we had that help, there would be less pressure on us to augment our number in order properly to carry out our duties. That is an interim step. The cost of constituency offices would be very small indeed compared with the cost we are ultimately going to

face by expanding the numbers in this House of Commons. I will return to that at the end of my remarks.
I want to indicate why I am concerned with the manner in which the Electoral Boundaries Commissions operate. I do not think they are responsive enough to across-the board needs, taking into account the historical and social considerations in constituencies. I ask Your Honour to bear with me while I refer specifically to my own constituency of Edmonton-Strathcona as a case in point.
In the period between 1968 and the beginning of this session in 1973, Edmonton-Strathcona was practically unheard from in the House of Commons. That is the second reason I am returning to that particular constituency. I want to indicate how it has been hurt, but not from the point of view of partisanship or politically, it does not make any difference because of the general situation in Alberta today with regard to politics. What I am referring to is the manner in which an arbitrary dissection of the historical riding of Edmonton-Strathcona has been made by crossing the North Saskatchewan river and bringing into Edmonton-Strathcona the southern part of the former Edmonton West constituency.
The point I am trying to make is this. Anyone who knows Edmonton knows how important the North Saskatchewan river is to the life of the city. You are either on the north or the south side of that river when in Edmonton. The community interest is greatly affected by that river. To draw an arbitrary line and destroy the integrity of a constituency with the name Strathcona, originating from the founding of the city of Strathcona, the terminal railway point between Calgary and Edmonton before there was any bridge across the Saskatchewan river, is to have very little regard for the community interests in Strathcona.
Even more important than that historical observation is the contemporary note that seems to summarize the problems we face in Canada today. I refer to a non-partisan group called the Strathcona Historical Society. It was founded about one year ago and is funded by the city of Edmonton to analyse the problems of old Strathcona which exists in the very heart of the former Strachcona riding on the south side of the city.
Today people are moving into this area. It is quickly becoming a high rise community. The commercial interests are very worried because there is no long range planning for the area. They are not sure exactly what should be done. The Strathcona historical group studied the problem for 10 months and brought in a plan for the revitalization of Edmonton-Strathcona.
This has a direct bearing on the subject of the bill before us because what this group has tried to do is to show that old Strathcona is a highly urbanized area in the process of change. The group wishes to reinforce not only the identity but the idea of old Strathcona as a commercial centre and as a residential community, as well as an arrival point; to create a sense of place, a focal point of a neighbourhood, one which gives a sense of community and so on.
They have drawn up a plan which would allow for the redevelopment of the area while preserving human values.
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension They propose in their plan a vision for the future of old Strathcona built on the environmental qualities and the architectural heritage of the area. Simultaneously the plan encourages an attitude toward future development which would be sympathetic to the preservation of the heritage and qualities of old Strathcona. By providing an image of a possible future, the plan is a way of encouraging the implementation of its own recommendations and objectives. As an alternative to the present ad hoc approach to urban renewal, the plan encourages not only the preservation of existing buildings but the reinforcement of a sense of place and provision of a method of continuity with the past, the present and the future.
When I appeared before the Electoral Boundaries Commission I brought with me representatives of the Strathcona historical group who were at that time concluding their report, and they, too, made a presentation to the Electoral Boundaries Commission in Alberta. In their presentation they pointed out the salient fact that the Electoral Boundaries Commission, in redrawing old Strathcona, had split old Strathcona right down the middle, drawing a line which anyone knowing Edmonton would think was imcomprehensible because it was drawn along the Canadian Pacific tracks. Then the line along the new constituency suddenly veered to the west along 82nd Avenue to 109th Street, thereby splitting 82nd Avenue in the heart of the old Strathcona community, the north side of 82nd Avenue or, as Edmonton calls it, White Avenue, being in the new riding of Edmonton-Strathcona, the south side being in the new riding of Edmonton South.
The community of interest was thereby broken. We tried in non-partisan terms to explain that the interests of the community of old Strathcona, which so many people are taking such pains to restore in a way which will be a credit to modern urban Canada, required us to plead with them to redraw the map and to draw the eastern boundary of Strathcona along Mill Creek Ravine or at least 99th Street, running right into the river, thereby preserving the integrity of the riding.
I must say in compliment to the Electoral Boundaries Commission that when I asked them to at least save the name of Edmonton-Strathcona they agreed to do this, but they put it on the wrong side of south Edmonton instead of keeping it where it should be, in the heart of the Strathcona area in order to keep the community of interest.
I have recounted these events tonight to illustrate why I believe that the government House leader was on the right track. I hope we will not allow ourselves to be detoured because of what might happen further down the road. It is my opinion he was on the right track when he said we must get something better in the way of redistribution. The only way I can think of to get anything better is to set up a new commission or, at least, to instruct the commission which exists to use broader terms of reference which we will provide in this House.
We need terms of reference which will not merely reflect the old slogan "rep by pop" but which will take into consideration social and historical situations as well as the modern situations we face. What we are hearing in this debate-and my hon. friend from Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) stated a number of different aspects of

Let us do this, though, in a way which is not rushed, in a way which will, in this decade of the 'seventies, serve the Canadian people better.

Mr. Speaker, I am against the passage of Bill C-208, an act to suspend the operations of the electoral boundaries act, because I do not believe the House has truly taken into account the effect of such a suspension.
Should Bill C-208 be passed, it would probably result in the country being in a state of confusion on this issue until 1978 or thereabouts. The wish of those supporting the bill is that the new electoral boundaries should not come into effect until after the next election. If, then, there is an election a year from now, 1974, and a majority government is in office for four years, it will be only when 1978 is reached the new boundaries will apply. Passage of this bill would therefore mean a continuation for five or more years of wrangling and insecurity, for there will never be agreement on where the boundaries should be. A change in boundaries which would satisfy one group of people will automatically cause dissatisfaction with another group of people. The more changes proposed, the more so-called solutions will be demanded.
Another consideration which should be taken into account, Mr. Speaker, is that after the next election each member of parliament would have to serve, or, at least, be alert to the needs of, two constituencies, the one in which he was elected and the one in which he would hope to be elected in the next election. There might be a temptation for some politicians after the next election to ignore the people in the section he presently represents because they would not be voting in the constituency he would represent in the next election. To avoid confusion, insecurity and divided loyalty the preliminary report of the Electoral

Boundaries Commission should be adopted by this House as soon as possible.
What about the provinces which would lose seats as a result of the adoption of the preliminary report? The solution is not to add 30 or more seats to the House of Commons, for if in 1978 we had about 294 seats, in 1988 we might have 400. Why not have 500 or more-bureaucracy compounded as we round the turn of the century? We who come from rural Saskatchewan sometimes think that when you are only standing still you are winning. I hope in the next 18 months to come up with a formula for representation by members of parliament in Ottawa that will be fair to everyone in Canada.
In the last 15 or 20 years our representation from Manitoba and Saskatchewan has fallen from 38 to the proposed 24 seats. This is a drop from 10 per cent of the members to 6V4 per cent. It is strange that traditionally from those areas very seldom are there government members. There is a feeling out there of alienation from the rest of Canada. The government has recognized that it has not dealt fairly with the west, and is now proposing to make amends shortly in Calgary. What purpose would be

served by insulting that region further by decreasing its representation in Ottawa?
I think an MP's role can be divided into two parts. The first is to serve the constituents. It has been mentioned by many people that we are increasingly supplying the people with more and more services, with lip and leap and you name it. Every time we do a service for a constituent we add more work for the member of parliament.
Hopefully, then, we can come up with a formula which would allow us on an equal basis to serve our constituents equally. It has been mentioned by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) that we are the delegates of the people, not of acres of land or miles of shoreline. Unfortunately, the acres of land, the miles of shoreline and geography all have a bearing on our ability to serve our constituents. A very important aspect of the service of a member of parliament to his constituents is his acceptability to the people.
Recently we have heard talk about offices in our constituencies. This talk has been promoted by urban members. In a rural constituency this would not be of much help. If we could assist a member of parliament to travel about 200 miles one must travel between meetings, then that would be of more help. Our office in a rural area is really our car. I travel 500 miles on a normal weekend trying to be of service to the people in my constituency. I do not think members with a city riding would drive that many miles in a session.

speechtext:
The other aspect of the role of an MP is a delicate one. Supposedly he comes here to represent the views of his constituents. If this delicate role was the only one we thought about, perhaps representation by population would be all right, but it is not. If we adopt the idea that an MP is l/265th of the House of Commons, then each person is sort of representing one in 80,000. That would work out very nicely if all we were doing here was representing the views of our constituents. It has been mentioned that representation by population is the formula presently used. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) said it was the law. I do not think it is the law. We do not divide the total population by 265, come up with a figure and then devise representation for each province. That is not the law at all.
The law is that certain provinces have been given guarantees under the constitution, and if they are taken care of and their requirements are met, the rest of the country is divided equally and then the country has representation by population. We now have a precedent, as has been mentioned in the debate, under the constitution. The province of New Brunswick cannot have fewer than 10 members of parliament. In addition, under the constitution any other province that has a population greater than New Brunswick cannot have fewer than 10 seats. So Saskatchewan and Manitoba could eventually fall to 10 seats.
We in Saskatchewan are unfortunately very close to the province of Alberta. For a reason which is obvious and requires no explanation, rapid growth in Alberta seems to take place at the expense of Saskatchewan. But the precedent has been established by the constitution that we cannot fall below 10 seats as long as our population
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Suspension remains higher than the population of New Brunswick. This is a strange law. We have 300,000 more people yet we are guaranteed by the constitution that we will have the same number of members of parliament.
I suggest there is lots of time in the next 18 months for us to devise a better formula. A far simpler solution would be to allow 10 members for New Brunswick, and for those provinces with declining populations allow one more member for each 100,000 population greater than New Brunswick. That would freeze Saskatchewan and Manitoba with the 13 members they presently have. The problem could be solved as simply as that, but this would require an adjustment and a change in the constitution.
Surely the constitution should serve us. We are masters of the constitution, not its servants. One could devise a much more complicated formula, but this would suffice for our purpose. If Saskatchewan gained 100,000 people and had a population of 400,000 more than the province of New Brunswick, we could possibly then have 14 seats. There is no reason the people in the west or on the Prairies should not be granted the same privileges and rights the people of New Brunswick have under the constitution. They may have been a little more astute at the time of confederation, but let us during the next 18 months be fair to all regions and all people of Canada. If we are to have representation by population, then let us have it. If it is to be done in some other way, fine, but let us be fair to everyone. I have no real quarrel with the way the map is drawn for Saskatchewan. The only quarrel I have is that if we drop from 13 seats to 12 seats, having had 21 not too long ago, this would be a bitter pill to take.
We, as well as others in rural Saskatchewan, are faced with the problem of sending better qualified people to Ottawa. The longer one remains a minority, the weaker one's voice becomes in the crowd. The trend is to the cities, and it is no wonder this is the situation because much of the legislation seems to force a move in that direction. We are legislated against in the rural areas time and time again. I shall not go into that here, but certainly I hope in the next 18 months, the time we are buying by supporting this bill, we will come up with something that will be more fair to the rural areas.

It is precisely for that reason that we must be concerned about the way in which there is a threat posed by the bill regarding the urban dwellers of this country being adequately represented. The people are not simply individuals isolated and living on their own. They too are members of communities which have concerns, needs and ambitions. They too have need for adequate representation, representation which they have lacked very much in this House of Commons and in the councils associated with it.
The great values of being adequately represented in this House of Commons is not simply that there is someone here who responds to your individual requests for assistance with pensions, unemployment insurance and other matters. It is that there is someone here who speaks up for your community and voices the needs, ambitions and legitimate desires of those communities in Parliament, in caucus, in committee and in the various other ways in which Parliament carries on its business.
It is for that reason that I believe we must be very seriously concerned about the urban communities of this country being given adequate representation. At the present time they are under-represented. The real and basic principle of democracy is the right of individuals to representation according to their numbers. There have been certain remarks even in this debate tonight in which the integrity and validity of the principle of "rep by pop" has been questioned. But this is a principle on which the whole membership of this Parliament is based, one we must honour and honour in the way in which we address ourselves to the challenge of redistribution.
It is only common sense that when a democratic body such as this House of Commons is drawn up, it will be based upon the way in which the population is distributed across the country. This common sense has clearly not occurred to all members here. Surely this ought to be something that every member would accept as a fair and just way of giving every Canadian that to which he is entitled, and that is adequate and fair representation in the Parliament which governs his land.
At the present time there are great numbers of Canadians in the urban areas of this country, including my own, which are under-represented and which do not have the opportunity for an equal voice in the Parliament of Canada. This is an intolerable situation and something with which Parliament must not be content. We know that in the British North America Act redistribution is something that is guaranteed to the people. It would seem that this constitutional guarantee is now being thwarted. Certainly it is in danger of being thwarted. We in this House ought not to be content with a proposal that would rob the people of the country of something their basic constitution gives them.
I hope, therefore, we will begin to think in terms of what is fair to all people of this country who have in large numbers chosen to live in urban areas. No one persuaded them to do this. No one led them by the hand to come to the big cities. They themselves chose to live there. Having so chosen they should have the right to be adequately

represented from those areas in the Parliament of this country.
Might I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address some remarks to all hon. members tonight concerning the Department of National Defence lands in Vancouver known as Jericho lands.
I think in starting out I might remind all hon. members of some of the history of this. In 1942 when this country was at war the Department of National Defence acquired by lease 172 acres of land used for recreational purposes in the city of Vancouver. In 1947 the Department of National Defence was able to buy the land at a very low price. By 1965 the leader of the government during that abortive election campaign made promises about returning some of the land to the city of Vancouver, and by 1968 the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) agreed that this land should be returned to recreational purposes.
By 1969 this governement had maintained its word up to a point; 72 acres of the total 172 had been returned to Vancouver. But the Department of National Defence retained 62 acres. There was also another 38 acres of defence land which the Department of National Defence did not return. The reason put forward was that this had to cover the cost of moving the defence establishment to some other place.
The plan of the Department of National Defence to be foisted on the citizens of Vancouver was that we should have a high rise, in spite of the fact that this was against all our ideas, hopes and dreams for that particular property in that particular place. None the less, the Department of National Defence persisted with this inane idea because some internal auditor in the Department of National Defence had to somehow balance the books-a balancing act that never bothered the government too much in other ways. The government insisted that this land, which is owned by all taxpayers of Canada, and certainly by myself and other hon. members, could not be returned to the city of Vancouver because, for some reason which made no sense to anybody and which was never explained to the citizens of Vancouver in any coherent form, the Department of National Defence used it to pay for the move of defence establishments many years after the war was over.

The question which the citizens of Vancouver are asking is: Why don't we get this land back? On January 26 my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), raised a question in the House of Commons, to which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) replied:
There is an agreement in existence between the government and the city of Vancouver. My predecessor has indicated that if the city wishes to reopen this agreement we would certainly be prepared to do so and to listen to representations.
Why was there an agreement? There was an agreement for only one reason-because the government said to the citizens of Vancouver that they cannot have the land back, that they will have to find some way to pay the department for the move. That is why there was agreement and the government took this attitude. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), who is here tonight, says "and so did the Auditor General". My point is this, that if the government concerns itself with urban affairs and is prepared to spend $33 million of government money-your money and mine-to acquire parkland in the city of Toronto, to which I have no objection, then why is this government so constipated in its imagination that it cannot find its way to transfer this defence land back?
If the argument which the minister has put forward is valid, why did the government return the 72 acres to the city of Vancouver? Because surely the same argument would apply. The fact of the matter is that this government is acting in a parsiminious, stupid, and ostrich-like way. It keeps on wondering and holds conferences to discover why the west is "brassed off". If ever there was an expression that puts it in a nutshell, that is it.
This matter may not be earth shattering, but if any member on the government side wants to know why they lost the riding of Vancouver Quadra, apart from the fact that the hon. member who now holds it worked very hard, let him go and ask the former member about the Jericho land.
This was the symbol of the kind of neglect to which we have been subjected by a centralized government that does not care about the west and does not have sufficient sensitivity to pay attention to the commonsense things that people tell it to listen to. I am startled and surprised at the fact that another hon. member from the same city from which I come can sit here and quibble at me from across the floor and try to defend the government's position.
This matter has been raised consistently in the House by my friend the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. He raised it on February 27 and again on June 13, as recorded in Hansard. It was raised again on June 21, this time by my friend and colleague the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). She asked the government for the reason for the double standard-which is the word I used later when I brought it up in the House-in the treatment of Toronto and Vancouver. This is the answer that the minister gave, as reported in Hansard of June 21:
Mr. Speaker, I am certain the hon. member knows that this matter is under negotiation . . .
This is the only answer we ever get. The reason it is under negotiation is that the government is not prepared to return the land. The government wants its pound of
Adjournment Debate
flesh out of it. There would be no negotiation, there would be no agreement, Mr. Speaker, if that were not the position that the government had taken. The matter was again raised on July 6 by the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), as reported in Hansard, and it had been previously raised by me on June 29.
To add insult to injury, Mr. Speaker, here is an article in the Vancouver Sun of July 7 referring to a statement of another hon. member from Vancouver, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford). The article reports him as saying:
. . . the federal government would be willing to meet with Vancouver city council to discuss the possibility of a federal-provincial housing complex on the 38 acres of Jericho land owned by the federal government.
If after all these years that is the way the government is thinking, then we are not being told the proper story. Mr. Speaker, I insist that tonight I receive from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hopkins) some complete and proper answers to these questions. We have been waiting for 20 years to get this land back and the people of my city are fed up.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter raised by the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) has been the subject of many questions in the House. On March 25, 1969, the Department of National Defence signed an agreement with the city of Vancouver governing the usage of approximately 140 acres of what is commonly known as the Jericho Beach property. The terms of this agreement provided for the turning over to the city of, for the sum of one dollar, 73 acres of waterfront property to be used as parkland.
As part of this agreement, the remaining 38 acres was rezoned as CD1-that is a "comprehensive development district". The zoning classification was selected by the city and permits the construction of garden homes and town houses. The opinion expressed at the time was that this zoning would enhance rather than detract from the surrounding community. For the record, this land was acquired from the province of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver during and immediately following World War II for either straight market value or the exchange of lands of equal value. The turnover of the 73 acres of waterfront property to the city of Vancouver is now complete.
I should like also to point out that the Department of National Defence has in the past made available to the city of Vancouver some very substantial land holdings. Stanley Park, consisting of over 900 acres, is on long-term lease to the city.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
speechtext: How many hundred years do you want to go back?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
speechtext:
Valuable properties at Kitsilano Beach were turned over to the city. Other smaller properties have also been made available for the city's use. And now some 73 acres of very valuable waterfront have been handed over for only token consideration.
One cannot resist speculating on what the current market value of the total properties turned over by DND

July 9, 1973
Adjournment Debate
to the city of Vancouver would be worth today. However, the city of Vancouver has, through its dealings with the Department of National Defence, acquired substantial park acreage at virtually no cost.
The member for Vancouver South raises the issue of federal support to the city of Toronto for the acquisition of parkland. This was not DND land and is not related in any way to DND policy.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
speechtext: What difference does it make?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-JERICHO DEFENCE LAND, VANCOUVER-GOVERNMENT TERMS FOR TRANSFER TO CITY
speechtext:
What is at issue is the Department of National Defence policy for the disposal of property, in this case to the city of Vancouver. These two matters are not related and should not be confused.
As a result of recent representations to the Department of National Defence by a few Vancouver citizens and detailed discussions with the city, the department has delayed the approved development of the remaining 38 acres. Departmental officials are currently discussing, with both city and provincial officials, various options for the future disposition of approved Jericho Beach development property. The department expects within the next two weeks to receive a proposal from the city of Vancouver.
Needless to say, any reasonable proposal concerning the remaining Jericho Beach property will receive serious consideration.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN-POSSIBILITY OF LOWERING PENSIONABLE AGE TO 60-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN-POSSIBILITY OF LOWERING PENSIONABLE AGE TO 60-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 18, as recorded in Hansard at page 4840, I put a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) as follows:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the discussions that took place earlier in this session, but which were never finalized, concerning the possibility of lowering the pensionable age under the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to age 60, will the minister before the end of this session be making a statement on this matter?
The minister's reply was given to me in a very friendly manner but, even so, the answer was no. I then put a supplementary question to the minister asking if he would give consideration to the question of lowering the pensionable age as a priority measure during the lifetime of this parliament. The minister answered that he had been prepared to discuss the matter when his estimates were before the standing committee but that the standing committee chose otherwise. He concluded his reply with this sentence as found at page 4841 of Hansard:
This question is one that is being considered with all the other issues concerning the review of social security that is taking place with the provinces at the present time.
I have no doubt that it is because of that sentence that the parliamentary secretary, in preparing to make a reply tonight, has brought with him that orange book which of course outlines all of the matters in the field of social security that are now under discussion.

I raise this issue tonight not because I have anything new to say. It is simply a plain ordinary fact that the time has come for the eligible age for pensions under both the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to be lowered to age 60.1 believe that the people of Canada want and are ready for this kind of change to be made. They are prepared that it be done on a voluntary basis-in other words that such pensions shall be paid to those persons who are prepared to withdraw from the labour market. But I am convinced that the people of Canada want action in this field.
What concerns me very much is that in the earlier part of this session, during the time the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne was being debated and we were anticipating and waiting for the legislation respecting old age pensions, a great deal was said about this matter. It was said not just by some of us in this corner of the House but by hon. members to my right from the Progressive Conservative Party, and by many Liberal members sitting on the government side of the House. They urged that the pensionable age be lowered. If it could not be done for everyone they urged that it be done for spouses of pensioners or they urged that the age be brought down from age 65 to 64, to 63, to 62, to 61 and to 60.
I am sure that all hon. members will confirm that during those first couple of months of this session a great deal was said on this issue. But once the debate on the Speech from the Throne was over, and once the Old Age Security Act amendments had been brought in raising the basic pension to $100 a month and raising the amount of the supplement, very little continued to be said on this issue, except by a few of us who will not let it be forgotten.
I am concerned that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his colleagues in the government may now think it is a quiet issue and that they do not need to be worried about it. I tell the minister, I tell the government, and I tell my good friend from St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) who is applauding what I am saying, that this issue will not die down. When the next election campaign comes along one of the questions that will be asked of members of all parties is this: "Why didn't you bring down the eligible age for pensions to age 60?"
It is nice to know that there are discussions on this question between the federal government and the provinces. It is nice to know that there are references to the lowering of the eligible age in that orange book entitled "A Working Paper on Social Security in Canada". But things that are the subject of discussion, things that get into white papers, working papers, white books and green books, have a way of surviving for a long time. I still have in my files a copy of the 1919 Liberal convention program and platform and I am still waiting for some of those 1919 proposals to be implemented.
What we want is not just discussion about this matter, not just the assurance that something will be done some day, that it is being considered along with all the other issues. We want the government to realize that in the seventies the people of Canada believe that the time has come for pensions to be made available at age 60, and we want action on this at an early date. We want it now.
July 9, 1973

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-OLD AGE SECURITY ACT AND CANADA PENSION PLAN-POSSIBILITY OF LOWERING PENSIONABLE AGE TO 60-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). As he said, he did not propose to say anything new. He has been talking about pensions in this House for a long time. I think all people would say he has represented pensioners very well.
It is quite true when he remarks there are members, not only in his party but on this side of the House and in other parties, who have taken a great deal of interest, particularly in the last couple of years, in the reduction of the pensionable age. In all fairness, I should say that in spite of the importance that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre attaches to this question, it is a complicated matter in that there are priorities to be considered. In our work paper on social security a number of other urgent social problems are brought to bear as well.
We in the department believe it is important that the provinces be consulted in these matters. They are now being consulted. The minister has indicated the interest he has in this subject. As the hon. member knows, he was quite willing to discuss the matter fully with the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs when the estimates were before that committee, and we attach a great deal of importance to this.
I point out to the hon. member that by adding those from age 60 to 64 to the pensionable age would add 801,000 people to the present number of 1,782,000 pensioners. That is a lot of people. It involves an enormous expenditure of funds, estimated to be in the billions of dollars. When one looks at the amount received by those who are now pensionable related to minimum wages in the provinces or to that which can be obtained under social assistance, one finds those who are pensionable are earning more than many who are working for a living in Canada today.
These things all have to be taken into consideration and put into their proper perspective. The provinces need to have some input in terms of their priorities as well. The department is very much concerned about this problem. It is looking at it in an active way and is in the process of discussing it and other social priorities at the present time. Hopefully something will be done which will benefit the maximum number of people in this country in the best possible way.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-TORONTO TERMINAL No. 2-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PLANS TO IMPROVE
AIRPORTS-TORONTO TERMINAL No. 2-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PLANS TO IMPROVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 5 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to report on his activities with regard to new plans to improve terminal No. 2 at Toronto International Airport. The minister said in an offhand manner he had answered the question before. I checked in Hansard my question to the minister of June 15, approximately three weeks before. At that time I asked the minister about plans for expanding terminal No. 2. The minister replied the terminal was to be built in three stages and there were plans to extend the terminal, but he was not going to let anyone see them. They were his private affair.
Adjournment Debate
Earlier the same day the minister said he did not build the terminal himself. A lot of people are unhappy about it, but the minister said not to blame him because he did not build it. The minister said he would not let anyone see the plans for improving the terminal. He said he knows it is an abortion, but it does not matter because it is only the Canadian public that uses it. As Air Canada says, the terminal is for our travelling convenience.
The minister said that when the terminal was built, it was decided it was good for people to walk half a mile before getting on an airplane. If this was a railway terminal the railways would be out of business. If it were a hog terminal the pigs would die of exhaustion. This was supposed to be a freight terminal. Because the government airline has no policy to control these things, it was forced to take over this freight terminal. We now have a freight shed being used as a terminal for people. It is a great terminal. It is true the floor is of cold concrete but there are some pastel colours on the walls. Aside from that, there is nothing modern about it if one excepts the modular steel chairs in the ante-rooms, so uncomfortable that no one can sit on them for more than two or three minutes before getting up to take a walk. There are no newspaper stands, no bars, no decent washrooms, not even a smoke-shop or a book stall. So unless a person is prepared, having got there, to walk back half a mile to buy a book or a newspaper, he can sit on one of those modular steel chairs and stare at the walls.
I am glad the parliamentary secretary is here to reply to me tonight because I know he enjoys travelling to Toronto and using terminal No. 2 with its excellent conveniences. Once upon a time-and this was in the good old days- airports were so designed that a traveller who had parked his car at an airport had no need to go outside in the open when the time came to use it again. But in keeping with modern design, cars now have to be parked as much as half a mile away so that on rainy or snowy days visitors have the privilege of walking outside and, later, sending their clothes to be dry-cleaned.
Sooner or later, the airlines realized that the corridor was some 1400 or 1500 feet long and that it would be nice to have electric current cars to make the journey. So they obtained two of these cars. Because they are powered by batteries, one car has always to be tied to the charging system. The other is usually employed to transfer Air Canada personnel to their places of work in the terminal- it seems to serve no other purpose. So this terminal is designed to be tough on the person suffering from a heart condition, tough on the woman taking her children on holiday, perhaps having to carry a child 1500 feet, tough on the businessman carrying a heavy case, and tough, even, on the hon. parliamentary secretary when he is carrying his bag. In short, it is cardiac alley.
The Ministry of Transport has not yet got enough sense to recognize this fact and do something about it. No, their idea is to make it longer. The have planned it that way. They have not shown to the public in Toronto or the rest of the country that they possess any initiative whatsoever. They know the terminal is a horror show. They know it is improperly designed and a danger to people using it. But

July 9, 1973
Adjournment Debate
they intend to extend it anyway because after all, there is a plan to extend it.
Instead of coming out with real leadership and admitting that this terminal is wrong, instead of acknowledging that people cannot be expected to use facilities of this kind, the minister says: Well, I have answered that question once, and I am not going to answer it again. In fact, he has no answers. The ministry has no answers. The government has no answers.
I say this to you, Mr. Speaker: the people of Toronto know the government has no answers. They know it every time they go to terminal No. 2. They know the tragedy caused by lack of leadership in this country. They know the way Air Canada has been abused, and they realise, when they see this airport and note its lack of facilities, that the government does not really care about Canadians and does not care about the travelling public. So much is obvious, because otherwise they would not put up with the kind of operation carried on at terminal No. 2. in Toronto. I hope the parliamentary secretary has some good answers for us tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-TORONTO TERMINAL No. 2-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON PLANS TO IMPROVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have the answer. The problem is that the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) is not giving the new building a chance to work out the difficulties inherent in an entirely new operation the size of this one. We cannot agree with any of the comments he has made.
It is obvious from the hon. member's comments that he does not know terminal 2. Terminal 2 was originally multi-airline designed, primarily to serve wide-bodied aircraft, and not designed for exclusive Air Canada use. It became apparent before the building was completed that the original design was out of date and that Air Canada should either operate totally from terminal 1 or the new terminal 2. Careful study by both Air Canada and the ministry of transport led to the decision in May, 1972, that Air Canada's operations should be totally from terminal 2.
With this change in plan substantial additions and modifications had to be carried out to meet Air Canada's
requirements. This was done. The terminal is still not large enough for Air Canada's total gate requirements in the summer peak, and it will have to be expanded further, as was allowed for in the original plan.
The building has a number of excellent new features and systems; single-stop check-in so that any passenger can check in at any counter position with no need for further check-in at the gate; separate and much improved ticket sales areas; a special large wing for domestic flights open only to passengers; an automated baggage conveyor and sorter; a much larger Rapidair lounge area and curbside baggage check-in, to name a few of the items for the benefit of people travelling.
The difficulties of opening day were substantial, and this was expected; but steady and rapid improvements have taken place as contractors have finished delayed installation, as the usual bugs were eliminated from new systems, and as the public and staff became more familiar with the layout.
Planned phased staff increases by Air Canada have taken place, as have improvements to facilities both in the terminal building and its adjacent parking facility. Improvements to the inter-terminal bus service have been implemented and a courtesy bus service from the Terminal 2 parking lot is now operating. The tunnel linking terminals 1 and 2 will be in operation by mid-August. I suggest this was not taken into consideration by the hon. member.
Ministry and airline officers have co-operated in the identification of problems and in the solution of these problems. Observations made over the July 1 weekend of peak period operations revealed a smooth traffic flow with no serious delay areas. The status of correction of some past major problem areas is signage, aesthetics, walking distance and road signs, and if I have time I should like to go into that particular aspect.
